items.stem: Two parallel metal plates in a vacuum are 0.055 m apart, with a potential difference of 2200 V between them. A singly charged potassium ion (m = 6.49 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, q = +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) starts from rest and accelerates across the uniform electric field. Neglecting gravity, calculate the speed of the singly charged potassium ion when it reaches the 0 V plate.
items.workedSolution: By conservation of energy, ½mv² = qV, so v = √(2qV / m) = √(2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2200 / 6.49 × 10⁻²⁶) = 1.04 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (B).

markScheme.criterion: Equates ½mv² = qV to obtain v = 1.04 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: Two point charges of +7 nC and +3 nC are fixed 0.7 m apart in a vacuum, with +7 nC on the left. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.3 m from the left charge. Use 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Both positive sources repel a positive test charge placed at P, so the left charge pushes rightward while the right charge pushes leftward. (b) |E₁| = k|q₁|/(0.3)² = 699 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/(0.4)² = 169 N C⁻¹. Subtracting the opposing vectors yields 531 N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: States that a positive test charge between like-sign sources experiences opposite forces from the left and right charges.
Evaluates E = k|q|/r² at r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.4 m.
Subtracts the two opposing field magnitudes.
Obtains 531 N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: Two point charges, +4 nC on the left and −16 nC on the right, are fixed 1 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.2 m from the left charge. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and V = 0 at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) V = k(4 × 10⁻⁹/0.2 + -16 × 10⁻⁹/0.8) = 0 V. (b) At P both fields point to the right, giving E = 899 N C⁻¹ + 225 N C⁻¹ = 1.12 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes signed charges with r₁ = 0.2 m and r₂ = 0.8 m into V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂).
Obtains V = 0 V.
Applies inverse-square law E = k|q|/r² to both sources.
Adds the two electric field magnitudes.
Obtains 1.12 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates are 0.025 m apart in a vacuum, with a potential difference of 150 V across them. A charged particle (q = +4 × 10⁻⁸ C, m = 4 × 10⁻⁶ kg) moves from the positive plate to the 0 V plate. Neglect edge effects and gravitational forces.
items.workedSolution: (a) Uniform field E = V / d = 150 / 0.025 = 6.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹. (b) Work done by the field W = qV = (4 × 10⁻⁸)(150) = 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ J.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes V = 150 V and d = 0.025 m into E = V / d.
Obtains 6.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹.
Applies W = qV (or W = qEd).
Obtains 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ J.

items.stem: In a uniform electric field, three equally spaced parallel equipotential lines are 0.035 m apart. Their potentials from left to right are 340 V, 200 V, and 60 V. A charged bead of charge +2 × 10⁻⁸ C and mass 1.4 × 10⁻⁵ kg is released from rest on the 200 V line and moves horizontally without friction.
items.workedSolution: (a) E = (200 − 60) / 0.035 = 4.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right. (b) a = qE / m = 5.71 m s⁻². (c) Using ½mv² = q(140), v = 0.632 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Divides adjacent potential step by spacing s.
Obtains 4.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right.
Applies a = qE / m.
Obtains 5.71 m s⁻².
Equates ½mv² = q(140) or uses v² = 2as.
Obtains 0.632 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A gas-discharge cathode-ray tube must be pumped down to low gas pressure, rather than kept at atmospheric pressure or a hard vacuum. Why is low gas pressure needed to sustain a steady discharge glow?
items.workedSolution: A cold-cathode discharge needs a Goldilocks pressure: low gas pressure gives electrons a long enough mean free path to gain ionising energy, yet sufficient atoms remain to ionise and sustain bombardment.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that low gas pressure gives electrons a long enough mean free path to gain ionising energy.

options.label: A
options.text: Low pressure is needed only to stop the glass tube exploding under atmospheric pressure.
options.distractorRationale: Low pressure actually creates an inward pressure difference on the glass; its electrical role is lengthening the electron mean free path.

options.label: B
options.text: A perfect vacuum produces the brightest gas glow because no atoms block the cathode rays.
options.distractorRationale: With zero gas atoms in a cold-cathode tube there are no positive ions to bombard the cathode and no gas atoms to emit glow.

options.label: C
options.text: Gas molecules only become electrically conductive above 10 atmospheres of pressure.
options.distractorRationale: High pressure shortens the mean free path so electrons cannot reach ionisation energy between collisions.

options.label: D
options.text: At atmospheric pressure frequent collisions stop acceleration, whereas low gas pressure gives electrons a long enough mean free path to gain ionising energy, while enough gas remains to supply ionising positive ions.

items.stem: Two identical small spheres, each carrying a charge of $+3.0\text{ }\mu\text{C}$, are held $12.0\text{ cm}$ apart inside a solid dielectric slab of relative permittivity $\varepsilon_{\text{r}} = 6.00$ ($\varepsilon = \varepsilon_{\text{r}}\varepsilon_0$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $F = \frac{(3.0 \times 10^{-6})^2}{4\pi (6.00 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12})(0.120)^2} = 0.937 N$. (b) A steady-current solenoid generates uniform parallel magnetic field lines inside the air-core solenoid resembling a bar magnet outside. (c) Bring the negative rod near the sphere, briefly earth it so repelled electrons drain away, remove the Earth link first, then withdraw the rod: earthing allows electrons to move between Earth and the conductor leaving a permanent opposite net charge.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $F = q_1 q_2 / (4\pi \varepsilon_{\text{r}} \varepsilon_0 r^2)$ with $\varepsilon = 6.00\,\varepsilon_0$.
Correct force 0.937 N.
Describes uniform parallel magnetic field lines inside the air-core solenoid resembling a bar magnet outside.
Notes closed field loops emerging from N end and returning to S end.
Describes bringing rod near sphere and briefly connecting the sphere to Earth before removing rod.
Explains earthing allows electrons to move between Earth and the conductor leaving a permanent opposite net charge.

parts.prompt: Outline how an uncharged insulated metal sphere can be given a net positive charge using a negatively charged rod charged by friction, without touching the sphere with the rod.
parts.expectedAnswer: Hold the negative rod nearby to polarize the sphere, earth the far side so electrons flow to Earth, break the Earth connection, and then remove the rod; earthing allows electrons to move between Earth and the conductor leaving a permanent opposite net charge.
workingSteps: Bring negative rod near sphere to repel free electrons to far side.
Earth sphere briefly and disconnect before removing rod so earthing allows electrons to move between Earth and the conductor leaving a permanent opposite net charge.

items.stem: Two fixed point charges of −4 nC (left) and −8 nC (right) are separated by 0.6 m in free space. Point P is located 0.2 m from the left-hand charge. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², with zero potential at infinity. Determine the electric potential at point P.
items.workedSolution: Electric potential is a signed scalar: V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂) with r₁ = 0.2 m and r₂ = 0.4 m. Thus V = −180 V + (−180 V) = −360 V (C).

markScheme.criterion: Sums signed scalar potentials kq₁/0.2 + kq₂/0.4 = −360 V (C).

items.stem: Two point charges, −10 nC (left) and +5 nC (right), are held 0.75 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line joining them, 0.25 m to the right of the −10 nC charge. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Both individual electric field vectors at P point to the left (toward the negative left source and away from the positive right source), so they reinforce toward the left. (b) With r₁ = 0.25 m and r₂ = 0.5 m, |E₁| = 1.44 × 10³ N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = 180 N C⁻¹. Summing gives 1.62 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

markScheme.criterion: Explains using a positive test charge that both source fields at P act in the same direction.
Applies E = k|q|/r² with r₁ = 0.25 m and r₂ = 0.5 m.
Adds the two electric field magnitudes.
Obtains 1.62 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

parts.expectedAnswer: Both individual electric field vectors at P point to the left (toward the negative left source and away from the positive right source), so they reinforce toward the left.

workingSteps: |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 1.44 × 10³ N C⁻¹; |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 180 N C⁻¹.

items.stem: Two fixed point charges lie on the x-axis: +9 nC at x = 0 and −6 nC at x = 0.7 m. A small test charge of −1.8 nC is placed at point P, where x = 0.3 m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electric potential at infinity. What is the electric potential at P due to the two fixed charges?
items.workedSolution: Electric potential at P depends only on the source charges: V = k(q₁/0.3 + q₂/0.4) = 270 V + (−135 V) = 135 V (C).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = k(q₁/0.3 + q₂/0.4) = 135 V (C), independent of q_test.

items.stem: Two point charges, +12 nC on the left and −4 nC on the right, are fixed 0.4 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line to the right of both charges, 0.8 m from the +12 nC charge. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Calculate the magnitude and direction of the resultant electric field at point P.
items.workedSolution: Exterior point P is r₁ = 0.8 m to the right of +12 nC and r₂ = 0.8 − 0.4 = 0.4 m to the right of −4 nC. Superposing E_x = kq₁/r₁² + kq₂/r₂² gives 56.2 N C⁻¹ to the left (A).

markScheme.criterion: Uses r₁ = 0.8 m and r₂ = 0.4 m to obtain 56.2 N C⁻¹ to the left (A).

items.stem: Two point charges, +2 nC on the left and +8 nC on the right, are fixed 0.9 m apart in a vacuum. Calculate the distance from the +2 nC charge to the point between them where the resultant electric field is zero.
items.workedSolution: Equating opposing field magnitudes gives q₁/x² = q₂/(0.9 − x)², so (0.9 − x)/x = √(8/2). Solving yields x = 0.9 × √2/(√2 + √8) = 0.300 m (C).

markScheme.criterion: Equates kq₁/x² = kq₂/(0.9 − x)² to obtain x = 0.300 m (C).

items.stem: Two point charges, +10 nC on the left and +3 nC on the right, are fixed 0.7 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.3 m from +10 nC. A small test charge of −3 nC is placed at P without moving the fixed charges. Use the Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Calculate the resultant electric force on the −3 nC test charge.
items.workedSolution: At P (r₁ = 0.3 m, r₂ = 0.4 m), the resultant electric field is E = 830 N C⁻¹ to the right. Multiplying by q_test = −3 nC gives F = q_test E = 2.49 × 10⁻⁶ N to the left (B).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates E = 830 N C⁻¹ and F = qE = 2.49 × 10⁻⁶ N to the left (B).

items.stem: Outside a charged conducting dome, the radial electric field strength is E = 4.50 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ at r₁ = 0.20 m and E = 1.125 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ at r₂ = 0.40 m. Estimate the potential difference |ΔV| between r₁ and r₂ using the area of a single trapezium strip.

markScheme.criterion: Finds trapezium estimate |ΔV| = 5.62 × 10⁴ V.

items.stem: Three parallel equipotential lines lie in a uniform electric field, spaced 0.035 m apart. From left to right, their potentials are 280 V, 140 V, and 0 V. A particle of charge +3.5 × 10⁻⁸ C moves from the 280 V line to the 0 V line.

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE_p = q(V_final − V_initial) with ΔV = -280 V.
Obtains ΔE_p = −9.80 × 10⁻⁶ J (with correct sign).
Applies W_field = −ΔE_p = q(V_initial − V_final).
Obtains W_field = 9.80 × 10⁻⁶ J (with correct sign).

items.stem: A triply charged lithium nucleus of charge +3e approaches a stationary gold nucleus head-on. The nucleus has atomic number Z = 79 (charge +79e), and the distance of closest approach is r_min = 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and zero electric potential at infinity. What is the electric potential due to the gold nucleus at distance r_min?
items.workedSolution: Radial potential of the +79e nucleus is V = kZe / r_min = (8.99 × 10⁹ × 79 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) / (5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 2.07 × 10⁶ V (C).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = kZe / r_min = 2.07 × 10⁶ V (C).

items.stem: Two positive point charges are fixed on the x-axis in a vacuum: +4 nC at x = 0 and +36 nC at x = 0.8 m. Assume a vacuum with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero potential at infinity. Calculate the electric potential at the point between the charges where the resultant electric field is zero.
items.workedSolution: Zero field occurs at x = 0.8 × √4/(√4 + √36) = 0.200 m from +4 nC (and 0.600 m from +36 nC). Scalar potentials add: V = k(q₁/x + q₂/(d − x)) = 719 V (B).

markScheme.criterion: Finds x = 0.200 m and sums positive scalar potentials to obtain 719 V (B).

items.stem: In a Millikan experiment ($g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$, air viscosity $\eta = 1.81 \times 10^{-5}\text{ Pa s}$), an oil droplet of density 880 kg m⁻³ falls at a terminal speed of 1.10 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ with the electric field off. It is then held stationary by 717 V across plates separated by 12.0 mm.
items.workedSolution: (a) $r = 1.02 μm$. (b) $m = 3.90 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg$. (c) $Q = 6.40 × 10⁻¹⁹ C$, which is 4.0 excess electrons.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $6\pi\eta r v = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho g$ with $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Correct radius 1.02 μm.
Applies $m = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho$.
Correct mass 3.90 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg.
Uses $Q = mgd / V$ with $d = 0.0120\text{ m}$.
Correct charge 6.40 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Divides by $1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$ to conclude 4.0 excess electrons.

items.stem: Two widely separated conducting spheres of unequal radii $R_1$ and $R_2$ are linked by closing switch S on a thin conducting wire. What condition determines the final equilibrium state?
items.workedSolution: Electrons move along the connecting wire until ΔV = 0, so V₁ = V₂ and total charge Q = Q₁' + Q₂' is conserved. Therefore the correct statement is: When connected by a conducting wire charge flows until both conducting spheres reach the same electric potential with total charge conserved.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: when connected by a conducting wire charge flows until both conducting spheres reach the same electric potential with total charge conserved.

options.distractorRationale: Charge flows until potentials equalise, leaving more charge on the larger sphere (Q ∝ R).

options.distractorRationale: Equilibrium requires zero potential difference (equal V), not equal surface field E = V/R.

items.stem: Two point charges, +8Q on the left and +5Q on the right, are fixed a distance 3 x apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 2 x from the left charge. Write the magnitude of the resultant electric field at P in the form E = α kQ/x², where k is the Coulomb constant.
items.workedSolution: (a) The right positive charge produces a larger repulsive field magnitude at P than the left positive charge, so the net electric field points to the left. (b) α = |8/2² − 5/1²| = |2.00 − 5.00| = 3.00.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies resultant direction as to the left with valid reasoning.
Forms inverse-square terms 8/2² and 5/1².
Subtracts the opposing dimensionless field coefficients.
Obtains α = 3.00.

items.stem: Two point charges are fixed 0.6 m apart in a vacuum: q₁ = 4 × 10⁻⁹ C on the left and q₂ on the right. The net electric field is zero at a point between them, 0.2 m from q₁.
items.workedSolution: (a) q₁ and q₂ have the same sign so their fields oppose between them. (b) |q₂/q₁| = ((0.6 − 0.2)/0.2)² = (0.4/0.2)² = 4.00. (c) q₂ = +(4.00)(4 × 10⁻⁹ C) = +1.60 × 10⁻⁸ C.

markScheme.criterion: States same sign because fields must oppose in the region between the charges.
Uses |q₂/q₁| = ((d − x₀)/x₀)² with d − x₀ = 0.4 m.
Obtains 4.00.
Multiplies q₁ by ratio from (b) with positive sign.
Obtains q₂ = +1.60 × 10⁻⁸ C.

items.stem: Between two large parallel charged plates separated by a small gap, equipotential lines drawn at equal voltage intervals are parallel and equally spaced. What does this uniform spacing show?
items.workedSolution: Since field strength equals the negative potential gradient so more closely spaced equipotentials indicate a stronger field, equal spacing corresponds to a constant field strength. Therefore the correct statement is: It shows constant uniform electric field because field strength equals the negative potential gradient so more closely spaced equipotentials indicate a stronger field

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: field strength equals the negative potential gradient so more closely spaced equipotentials indicate a stronger field.

options.text: It shows constant uniform electric field because field strength equals the negative potential gradient so more closely spaced equipotentials indicate a stronger field

options.text: It shows electric potential is identical everywhere between the two plates.
options.distractorRationale: Potential varies linearly from one plate to the other; only the gradient is constant.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows electric field strength falls off as inverse distance squared from the positive plate.
options.distractorRationale: Equal equipotential spacing implies constant E = V/d, not 1/r² decay.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows zero electrostatic force acts on an electron placed midway between the plates.
options.distractorRationale: A constant non-zero field exerts a constant force F = qE.

items.stem: A laboratory parallel-plate capacitor with air between its plates is charged to 18.0 V and disconnected from the supply before inserting a polar mica slab (εᵣ = 4.50). The overlapping plate area is 180 cm², plate separation is 1.20 mm, and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) C' = 597 pF. (b) 4.00 V. (c) E' = 4.78 nJ. (d) polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity.

markScheme.criterion: Converts cm² and mm to SI units in C = ε₀ εᵣ A / d.
Calculates C' = 597 pF.
Recognises isolated Q is constant so V' = V₀ / εᵣ.
Obtains 4.00 V.
Calculates final stored energy E' = 4.78 nJ.
States polar molecules rotate so negative ends face the positive plate.

Explains opposing internal field lowers net field and raises capacitance (polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity).

items.stem: Gravitational potential at any finite distance from a planet is always negative. Why can electric potential around an isolated charged sphere be either positive or negative?
items.workedSolution: Both obey inverse-square laws with zero potential at infinity, but gravitational force is always attractive with negative potential whereas electric force can attract or repel with positive or negative potential. Therefore the correct statement is: Taking zero potential at infinity, both obey inverse-square laws with zero potential at infinity, but gravitational force is always attractive with negative potential whereas electric force can attract or repel with positive or negative potential

options.label: A
options.text: Taking zero potential at infinity, gravitational potential is defined at the centre of Earth rather than at infinity.
options.distractorRationale: Both radial gravitational and radial electric potentials define zero at infinity.

options.label: B
options.text: Taking zero potential at infinity, gravity is weaker than magnetism so its potential is assigned a negative label arbitrarily.
options.distractorRationale: The negative sign follows physically from doing positive external work to separate attractive masses to infinity.

options.label: C
options.text: Taking zero potential at infinity, both obey inverse-square laws with zero potential at infinity, but gravitational force is always attractive with negative potential whereas electric force can attract or repel with positive or negative potential

options.label: D
options.text: Taking zero potential at infinity, electric charges cannot attract each other so electric potential is always positive.
options.distractorRationale: Unlike charges attract, giving negative electric potential around a negative source charge.

items.stem: In a hydrogen atom, a proton (1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) and an electron (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg), each of charge magnitude 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, are 5.30 × 10⁻¹¹ m apart. Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the ratio F_e / F_g.
items.workedSolution: F_e / F_g = e² / (4πε₀ G m_p m_e) = 2.26 × 10³⁹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds proton-electron force ratio 2.26 × 10³⁹.

items.stem: A student charges an air-gap capacitor from a constant-voltage DC supply through a resistor R. With the battery still connected, the student slides a polar polymer dielectric slab (εᵣ > 1) into the gap.
items.workedSolution: When charging from 0 to Q at fixed supply emf V, the battery supplies energy Q V while the capacitor stores half Q V, so exactly fifty percent is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of resistance value (a larger R slows current so charging takes longer, keeping ∫I²R dt = ½QV unchanged). Sliding the polar polymer into the gap causes its permanent molecular dipoles to rotate so negative ends face the positive plate and positive ends face the negative plate. These aligned dipoles set up an opposing internal electric field that tends to reduce the net field and plate potential difference; because the battery holds V constant across the plates, extra charge flows onto the plates until net field returns to V/d, raising C by εᵣ and increasing stored energy E = ½CV² by factor εᵣ.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: States that the constant-emf battery transfers total work W = QV while the capacitor stores E = ½QV (area under linear V–Q graph).
L1b: Concludes that exactly 50% (½QV) is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of the value of R.
L2a: Explains that polar polymer molecules rotate to align their negative ends toward the positive plate and positive ends toward the negative plate.
L2b: States that aligned dipoles create an opposing internal electric field inside the slab.
L3a: Explains that because the battery maintains fixed potential difference V, additional charge flows from the supply onto the plates to restore V = Ed.
L3b: Concludes that Q, capacitance C = ε₀εᵣA/d, and stored energy E = ½CV² all increase by factor εᵣ.

parts.prompt: Explain why half the energy supplied during the initial charging stage is always lost as thermal energy regardless of R, then explain microscopically why inserting the polar polymer causes additional current to flow from the battery and increases the stored electrical energy.
parts.expectedAnswer: When charging from 0 to Q at fixed supply emf V, the battery supplies energy Q V while the capacitor stores half Q V, so exactly fifty percent is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of resistance value (a larger R slows current so charging takes longer, keeping ∫I²R dt = ½QV unchanged). Sliding the polar polymer into the gap causes its permanent molecular dipoles to rotate so negative ends face the positive plate and positive ends face the negative plate. These aligned dipoles set up an opposing internal electric field that tends to reduce the net field and plate potential difference; because the battery holds V constant across the plates, extra charge flows onto the plates until net field returns to V/d, raising C by εᵣ and increasing stored energy E = ½CV² by factor εᵣ.
workingSteps: Explain 50% thermal loss via battery work QV vs triangular stored energy ½QV, independent of R.
Describe dipole alignment (− toward + plate) and opposing internal field.
Show why constant V draws additional charge from the battery, increasing C and stored energy by εᵣ.

items.stem: The diagrams show radial field lines and dashed circular equipotentials around a spherical planet of mass M and an isolated positive point charge +Q.
items.workedSolution: Both radial fields obey inverse-square laws with zero potential at infinity, but gravitational force is always attractive with negative potential whereas electric force can attract or repel with positive or negative potential. Gravitational field strength g = F/m = GM/r² acts radially inward toward mass M, whereas electric field strength E = F/Q = Q/(4πε₀r²) acts outward from +Q (inward toward −Q). In both fields, field strength equals negative potential gradient (g = −ΔV/Δr, E = −ΔV/Δr), equipotential surfaces are spheres centred on the source everywhere perpendicular to field lines, closer equipotentials indicate a stronger field, and zero work is done moving along an equipotential. Between subatomic particles such as two protons, electrostatic force exceeds gravitational force by ~10³⁶, while electric fields can be shielded by conductors whereas gravitational fields cannot.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: States both radial fields follow inverse-square laws (F ∝ 1/r², field ∝ 1/r²) with radial field lines and potential defined as zero at infinity.
L1b: States gravitational force acts on mass and is always attractive, whereas electric force acts on charge and can be attractive or repulsive.
L2a: Contrasts potential signs: gravitational potential V_g = −GM/r is always negative, while electric potential V_e = Q/(4πε₀r) is positive for +Q and negative for −Q.
L2b: States field strength equals the negative potential gradient (−ΔV/Δr) in both fields, so closely spaced equipotentials denote stronger fields.
L3a: Explains that equipotential surfaces intersect field lines at 90° and zero work is done moving a test mass or charge along an equipotential (ΔW = 0).
L3b: Notes the vast strength disparity at atomic scales (F_e/F_g ~ 10³⁶ for protons) and that electric fields can be shielded whereas gravitational fields cannot.

items.stem: Two point charges of −8 nC and −4 nC are fixed 0.8 m apart in a vacuum, with −8 nC on the left. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.3 m from the left charge. Use the Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the resultant electric field at point P?
items.workedSolution: Between like-sign charges, the individual fields at P oppose each other: |E₁| = k|q₁|/(0.3)² = 799 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/(0.5)² = 144 N C⁻¹. Subtracting gives |E_net| = 655 N C⁻¹ directed to the left (C).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts opposing inverse-square field contributions to obtain 655 N C⁻¹ to the left (C).

items.stem: Point charges +3 nC (left) and −6 nC (right) are fixed 0.6 m apart in a vacuum. Point P is between them, 0.2 m from the +3 nC charge. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electric potential at infinity. Although the electric potential at P is zero, determine the resultant electric field at P.
items.workedSolution: Even though V = kq₁/r₁ + kq₂/r₂ = 0 at P, the potential gradient dV/dx is non-zero because both opposite charges drive a positive test charge to the right: E = 674 N C⁻¹ + 337 N C⁻¹ = 1.01 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (C).

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes E != 0 when V = 0 and adds the field contributions along the line to obtain 1.01 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (C).

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates are 0.025 m apart in a vacuum and have a potential difference of 1000 V. A small charged particle (mass 2.8 × 10⁻⁶ kg, charge +1.4 × 10⁻⁸ C) moves from the positive plate to the earthed 0 V plate. Calculate the kinetic energy (in joules) gained by the particle across the 1000 V potential difference.
items.workedSolution: Electrical work done across the full potential difference is W = qΔV = (1.4 × 10⁻⁸)(1000) = 1.40 × 10⁻⁵ J (B).

items.stem: The graph shows how relativistic mass $m / m_0$ varies with $v / c$. An electron (rest mass $9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$, rest energy $0.511\text{ MeV}$) is accelerated to speed $v = 0.900c$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\gamma = 2.294 \Rightarrow m = 2.09 × 10⁻³⁰ kg$. (b) $E_{\text{k}} = 1.294 \times 0.511 = 0.661 MeV$. (c) At low speeds $m \approx m_0$, while relativistic mass approaches infinity as speed approaches c requiring infinite energy.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - 0.900^2} = 2.294$.
Correct relativistic mass 2.09 × 10⁻³⁰ kg.
Uses $E_{\text{k}} = (\gamma - 1) \times 0.511\text{ MeV}$.
Correct kinetic energy 0.661 MeV.
Notes $m \approx m_0$ at low speeds ($v \ll c$).
Explains relativistic mass approaches infinity as speed approaches c requiring infinite energy.

parts.prompt: Calculate the relativistic mass $m$ of the electron at $v = 0.900c$.
workingSteps: Multiply by $9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$ to obtain 2.09 × 10⁻³⁰ kg.

parts.prompt: Calculate the relativistic kinetic energy of this electron in MeV using $m_0 c^2 = 0.511\text{ MeV}$.
Describe how the relativistic mass graph behaves for $v \ll c$ and as $v \to c$, explaining the physical consequence.
parts.expectedAnswer: For $v \ll c$ mass stays almost constant at $m_0$ (agreeing with Newtonian mechanics), whereas relativistic mass approaches infinity as speed approaches c requiring infinite energy, setting $c$ as an unreachable speed limit for massive particles.
workingSteps: For $v \ll c$, $m \approx m_0$ matching classical mechanics.
State relativistic mass approaches infinity as speed approaches c requiring infinite energy.

items.stem: The diagram shows electric field lines and equipotential surfaces between two large oppositely charged parallel plates. What do the field lines near the outer edges of the plates indicate?
items.workedSolution: Between the central sections the field is uniform ($E = V/d$), whereas near the ends electric field lines bulge outward and spread apart near the plate edges showing a weaker non-uniform field.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that electric field lines bulge outward and spread apart near the plate edges showing a weaker non-uniform field.

options.label: A
options.text: Electric field lines bunch closer together near the edges, showing a stronger uniform field than at the centre.
options.distractorRationale: Wider spacing near the edges indicates weaker, not stronger, field strength.

options.label: B
options.text: Field lines cross over one another at the plate edges while equipotentials become parallel to the field lines.
options.distractorRationale: Electric field lines never cross, and equipotentials always cross field lines at right angles.

options.label: C
options.text: The electric field drops instantaneously to zero outside the geometric boundary of the plates.
options.distractorRationale: Real finite parallel plates have curved edge fields spreading outward beyond their geometric edges.

options.label: D
options.text: Edge effects occur where electric field lines bulge outward and spread apart near the plate edges showing a weaker non-uniform field compared with the uniform central region.

items.workedSolution: (a) Scalar potential V = k(q₁/0.2 + q₂/0.4) = 382 V. (b) Vector electric field E = 730 N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: Why is the relative permittivity εᵣ of any insulating polar dielectric slab always greater than unity?
items.workedSolution: Polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity. Therefore the correct statement is: Because in an applied field, polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity

options.text: Because polar molecules permanently amplify the electric field between the plates above the vacuum value.
options.distractorRationale: Aligned dipoles oppose rather than reinforce the applied field.

options.label: B
options.text: Because polar molecules increase the plate separation d inside the capacitor.
options.distractorRationale: Plate separation d is fixed by geometry.

options.label: C
options.text: Because in an applied field, polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity

options.label: D
options.text: Because free ions inside the insulator carry current straight from the positive plate to the negative plate.
options.distractorRationale: A dielectric is an insulator whose dipoles rotate in place without conducting through the gap.

items.stem: Two point charges are fixed on the x-axis: −2 nC at x = 0 and +6 nC at x = 0.4 m. Point P lies on the axis between them at x = 0.15 m. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Determine the magnitude and direction of the net electric field at point P.
items.workedSolution: At P, both opposite-sign sources drive a positive test charge to the left. |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 799 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 863 N C⁻¹ (with r₂ = 0.25 m). Summing the two same-sense vectors gives E = 1.66 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (D).

markScheme.criterion: Adds same-direction inverse-square contributions to obtain 1.66 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (D).

items.stem: Two point charges, +16 nC on the left and +4 nC on the right, are fixed 0.6 m apart in a vacuum.
items.workedSolution: (a) Between two positive charges their repulsive fields act in opposite directions, and equal field magnitudes require a smaller distance from the weaker right-hand charge. (b) Setting 16/x² = 4/(0.6 − x)² gives (0.6 − x)/x = √(4/16), hence x = 0.400 m.

Takes square roots correctly to linearize for x.
Obtains x = 0.400 m.

items.stem: Three parallel equipotential lines lie in a uniform electric field, spaced 0.05 m apart. From left to right, their potentials are -40 V, 60 V, and 160 V. A particle of charge +3 × 10⁻⁸ C moves from the -40 V line to the 160 V line. Calculate the signed change in electric potential energy ΔE_p of the charge.
items.workedSolution: Change in electric potential energy is ΔE_p = q(V_final − V_initial) = (+3 × 10⁻⁸ C)(160 − (-40)) = 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ J (B).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p = q(V_f − V_i) = 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ J (B).

items.stem: An alpha particle of charge +2e approaches a stationary zinc nucleus head-on. The nucleus has atomic number Z = 30 (charge +30e), and the distance of closest approach is r_min = 3 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and zero electric potential at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) V = kZe / r_min = 1.44 × 10⁶ V. (b) E_p = 2eV = 4.60 × 10⁻¹³ J. (c) Dividing by e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ gives 2.88 × 10⁶ eV.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes Q = 30e and r_min = 3 × 10⁻¹⁴ m into V = kQ/r.
Obtains 1.44 × 10⁶ V.
Multiplies potential from (a) by projectile charge 2e.
Obtains 4.60 × 10⁻¹³ J.
Divides joule energy by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ (or multiplies V in volts by z).
Obtains 2.88 × 10⁶ eV.

items.stem: Two positive point charges are fixed on the x-axis in a vacuum: +12 nC at x = 0 and +3 nC at x = 0.5 m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electric potential at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) Setting 12/x² = 3/(0.5 − x)² gives x = 0.333 m. (b) Scalar potentials add: V = k(q₁/x + q₂/(d − x)) = 485 V. (c) By definition of the null point (zero potential gradient), E = 0 N C⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Equates 12/x² = 3/(0.5 − x)².
Obtains x = 0.333 m.
Adds positive scalar potential contributions kq₁/x + kq₂/(d − x).
Obtains V = 485 V.
States 0 N C⁻¹.

items.stem: A negatively charged oil droplet is held stationary between horizontal plates, with the top plate positive. A brief burst of X-rays knocks one electron off the droplet. What happens to the droplet, and how must the plate voltage change to restore equilibrium?
items.workedSolution: Because $QV/d = mg$, losing an electron decreases upward electric force so a greater balancing potential difference is required to hold the droplet stationary again.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that losing an electron decreases upward electric force so a greater balancing potential difference is required.

options.distractorRationale: Removing an electron from a negatively charged droplet reduces the magnitude of its negative charge.

options.label: B
options.text: The droplet remains stationary because weight and viscosity are unaffected by X-rays.
options.distractorRationale: Reduced charge lowers upward electric force QV / d below weight mg, causing downward motion.

options.label: C
options.text: The droplet accelerates upward and requires a smaller potential difference to hold steady.
options.distractorRationale: With smaller Q, a larger V is needed to maintain QV / d = mg.

options.label: D
options.text: The droplet begins to fall because losing an electron decreases upward electric force so a greater balancing potential difference is required.

items.stem: A smooth Van de Graaff dome of radius 22.0 cm is at a potential of 36.0 kV ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F m}^{-1}$). It is then joined by a thin conducting wire to a distant uncharged sphere of radius 14.0 cm.
items.workedSolution: (a) C₁ = 24.5 pF. (b) E₁ = 15.9 mJ. (c) V_f = 22.0 kV. (d) total stored electrostatic energy decreases during charge sharing because energy is dissipated as thermal heating in the connecting wire and electromagnetic radiation.

markScheme.criterion: Converts radius to metres and applies C = 4πε₀R.
Obtains C₁ = 24.5 pF.
Applies E = ½CV² (or Q²/(8πε₀R)).
Obtains E₁ = 15.9 mJ.
Applies charge conservation Q = (C₁ + C₂)V_f with C ∝ R.
Obtains common potential V_f = 22.0 kV.
Notes total capacitance increases at fixed Q so E = Q²/(2C) drops.

Explains transfer to heat in wire and EM radiation (total stored electrostatic energy decreases during charge sharing because energy is dissipated as thermal heating in the connecting wire and electromagnetic radiation).

parts.prompt: Using $C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 R$, calculate the capacitance $C_1$ of sphere 1 in picofarads.
Calculate the electrostatic energy stored on sphere 1 before closing switch S, in millijoules.
Switch S is closed so the two spheres share charge until equilibrium. Calculate their final common potential in kilovolts.
Explain why the total electrostatic energy stored on both spheres after closing S is less than your answer to part (b).
parts.expectedAnswer: Energy is not retained electrostatically because total stored electrostatic energy decreases during charge sharing because energy is dissipated as thermal heating in the connecting wire and electromagnetic radiation.
workingSteps: total stored electrostatic energy decreases during charge sharing because energy is dissipated as thermal heating in the connecting wire and electromagnetic radiation.

items.stem: Two positive point charges, +12Q and +4Q, are fixed a distance 4 x apart in a vacuum, with +12Q on the left. Point P lies between them at a distance 2 x from +12Q. Using the Coulomb constant k, express the resultant electric field at P in terms of kQ/x².
items.workedSolution: At P, +12Q produces (12/2²) kQ/x² = 3.00 kQ/x² to the right, while +4Q at distance 2 x produces (4/2²) kQ/x² = 1.00 kQ/x² to the left. Net field = 2.00 kQ/x² to the right (D).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts (12/2²) and (4/2²) to obtain 2.00 kQ/x² to the right (D).

items.stem: Point charges q₁ = 7 × 10⁻⁹ C (left) and q₂ (right) are fixed 1.2 m apart in a vacuum. The resultant electric field is zero at a point between them, 0.4 m to the right of q₁. Calculate the signed value of charge q₂.
items.workedSolution: An interior null point requires q₁ and q₂ to have the same sign (+). Equating kq₁/x₀² = kq₂/(d − x₀)² with d − x₀ = 0.8 m gives q₂ = q₁((0.8)/(0.4))² = 4.00 × 7 × 10⁻⁹ C = +2.80 × 10⁻⁸ C (B).

markScheme.criterion: Uses q₂ = q₁((d − x₀)/x₀)² with positive sign to obtain +2.80 × 10⁻⁸ C (B).

items.stem: A small test charge is carried along a dashed circular equipotential contour around a fixed point charge. What geometric and energetic property holds everywhere on this path?
items.workedSolution: Since ΔW = qΔV and ΔV = 0 on an equipotential, equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential. Therefore the correct statement is: Everywhere in the field, equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential.

items.stem: An isolated air-spaced sensor capacitor charged to 24.0 V has its gap completely filled with a polar polymer sheet of relative permittivity 3.60. The overlapping plate area is 260 cm², plate separation is 0.900 mm, and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) C' = 920 pF. (b) 6.67 V. (c) E' = 20.5 nJ. (d) polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity.

workingSteps: C = ε₀ εᵣ A / d = 920 pF

parts.prompt: Calculate the new potential difference across the isolated plates after inserting the dielectric.
workingSteps: Isolated Q is unchanged ⇒ V' = V₀ / εᵣ = 24 / 3.6 = 6.67 V

parts.prompt: Calculate the final electrical energy stored by the capacitor in nanojoules.
Explain microscopically how the polar molecules inside the dielectric increase the capacitance.
parts.expectedAnswer: In the applied electric field, polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity.

items.stem: A spacecraft moves in a circular orbit around Mars with its engines switched off. Why does its speed stay constant even though Mars pulls on it continuously with a large gravitational force?
items.workedSolution: In circular orbit r is constant, and equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential. Therefore the correct statement is: Its circular orbit lies on a spherical equipotential: equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential.

options.text: Its engines must secretly cancel gravity because any non-zero force must change kinetic energy.
options.distractorRationale: A force perpendicular to velocity changes direction without changing speed or kinetic energy.

options.label: C
options.text: Gravitational force vanishes at orbital altitude so zero net force acts on the spacecraft.
options.distractorRationale: Gravitational pull provides the centripetal force keeping the spacecraft in orbit.

options.label: D
options.text: Its circular orbit lies on a spherical equipotential: equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential

items.stem: Two protons (mass 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge +1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) are separated by 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁰ m in vacuum. Using ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the ratio F_e / F_g of the electrostatic force to the gravitational force between them.
items.workedSolution: Since both forces vary as 1/r², r² cancels: F_e / F_g = e² / (4πε₀ G m_p²) = 1.23 × 10³⁶.

markScheme.criterion: Cancels r² to obtain ratio F_e / F_g = 1.23 × 10³⁶.

items.stem: The figure illustrates a parallel-plate capacitor filled with a polar dielectric slab alongside its linear Q–V charging graph.
items.workedSolution: polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity. In the applied electric field between the plates, polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity εᵣ. For an isolated capacitor (Q constant), the reduced net field lowers potential difference V = Ed by factor εᵣ, so C = Q/V rises by εᵣ and stored energy E = Q²/(2C) falls by εᵣ (work is done pulling the slab in). If kept connected to a constant-V supply, extra charge flows from the supply so Q and stored energy E = ½CV² both increase by factor εᵣ. During charging from empty at constant emf V, the battery transfers work W = QV, whereas the capacitor stores only the triangular area under the V–Q graph, E = ½QV; the remaining 50% (½QV) is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of the resistance value R.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: States that polar dielectric molecules rotate and align with their negative ends facing the positive plate and positive ends facing the negative plate.
L1b: Explains that the aligned dipoles produce an opposing (counter) internal electric field inside the dielectric.
L2a: Explains that the opposing internal field reduces the net electric field E between the plates.
L2b: Deduces for an isolated capacitor (fixed Q) that V = Ed decreases, so C = Q/V increases by factor εᵣ (and E_stored falls by εᵣ).
L3a: Contrasts battery-connected case (fixed V): extra charge flows from the supply so Q and stored energy increase by factor εᵣ.
L3b: Explains that charging at constant V draws W = QV from the battery while storing ½QV (area under V–Q graph), dissipating 50% (½QV) as heat in circuit resistance independent of R.

parts.prompt: Explain microscopically how inserting a polar dielectric increases the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor, contrast the effect on V, Q, and stored energy for an isolated versus battery-connected capacitor, and explain why charging a capacitor at constant supply voltage always dissipates 50% of the supplied energy as heat.
parts.expectedAnswer: polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity. In the applied electric field between the plates, polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity εᵣ. For an isolated capacitor (Q constant), the reduced net field lowers potential difference V = Ed by factor εᵣ, so C = Q/V rises by εᵣ and stored energy E = Q²/(2C) falls by εᵣ (work is done pulling the slab in). If kept connected to a constant-V supply, extra charge flows from the supply so Q and stored energy E = ½CV² both increase by factor εᵣ. During charging from empty at constant emf V, the battery transfers work W = QV, whereas the capacitor stores only the triangular area under the V–Q graph, E = ½QV; the remaining 50% (½QV) is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of the resistance value R.
workingSteps: L1: Polar molecule rotation/alignment (− end to + plate, + end to − plate).
L2: Aligned dipoles create an opposing internal electric field reducing net E between plates.
L3: Isolated (Q fixed → V falls → C = Q/V rises by εᵣ) vs connected (V fixed → extra Q flows) + 50% charging dissipation (½QV vs QV).

items.stem: Equipotential contours separated by equal steps ΔV are mapped around a spherical planet and around an isolated negatively charged sphere −Q.
items.workedSolution: equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential. Around both mass M and negative charge −Q, field lines point radially inward and potential is negative (approaching zero at infinity) because work must be done by an external agent to separate a test mass or positive test charge to infinity. In both maps, equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential (ΔW = mΔV or qΔV = 0). Because field strength equals negative potential gradient (−ΔV/Δr), equal-ΔV contours are tightly packed near the surface and spread further apart as 1/r² decreases. However, introducing a negative test charge near −Q reverses the force to repulsion (potential energy becomes positive), whereas gravity always attracts every mass regardless of composition; additionally, electrostatic forces vastly dominate on atomic scales and can be screened by a Faraday cage.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: Explains inward radial field lines and negative potentials around both M and −Q relative to zero at infinity.
L1b: States that external work must be done to move a test mass or positive test charge away from the centre to infinity.
L2a: Explains that equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines everywhere so ΔW = 0 along an equipotential.
L2b: Links increasing separation between equal-ΔV contours with distance to decreasing field strength via E = −ΔV/Δr (and g = −ΔV/Δr).
L3a: Contrasts sign behaviour: replacing +q with −q turns electrostatic force repulsive and makes potential energy positive, whereas gravity is always attractive for all masses.
L3b: Notes electrostatic fields are ~10³⁶ times stronger between subatomic particles and can be shielded by conductors, unlike gravity.

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates in a vacuum are 0.02 m apart, with a potential difference of 450 V between them. A charged silica sphere of charge +2.5 × 10⁻¹² C and mass 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ kg starts from rest at the positive plate and accelerates to the 0 V plate. Neglecting gravity, calculate the speed of the charged silica sphere when it reaches the 0 V plate.
items.workedSolution: By conservation of energy, ½mv² = qV, so v = √(2qV / m) = √(2 × 2.5 × 10⁻¹² × 450 / 5 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 2.12 m s⁻¹ (A).

markScheme.criterion: Equates ½mv² = qV to obtain v = 2.12 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: Two point charges, +4 nC (left) and +16 nC (right), are held 0.8 m apart along a straight line. Point P lies between them, 0.5 m from the +4 nC charge. Use the Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Both positive sources repel a positive test charge placed at P, so the left charge pushes rightward while the right charge pushes leftward. (b) |E₁| = k|q₁|/(0.5)² = 144 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/(0.3)² = 1.60 × 10³ N C⁻¹. Subtracting the opposing vectors yields 1.45 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

markScheme.criterion: States that a positive test charge between like-sign sources experiences opposite forces from the left and right charges.
Evaluates E = k|q|/r² at r₁ = 0.5 m and r₂ = 0.3 m.
Subtracts the two opposing field magnitudes.
Obtains 1.45 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

items.workedSolution: Unlike thermionic electron guns, a cold-cathode gas-discharge tube operates because positive gas ions accelerate into the cold cathode knocking out electrons as cathode rays.

options.label: A
options.text: A heated tungsten filament boils electrons off purely by thermionic emission in an ultra-high vacuum.
options.distractorRationale: Thermionic emission uses a heated filament in a vacuum; cold-cathode discharge tubes rely on gas ionisation and positive-ion bombardment.

options.label: B
options.text: High electric field ionises residual gas atoms so positive gas ions accelerate into the cold cathode knocking out electrons as cathode rays toward the anode.

options.label: C
options.text: Positive ions pass straight through the solid cathode and turn into negative electrons inside the wire.
options.distractorRationale: Positive ions strike the cathode surface and knock out surface electrons rather than turning into electrons.

options.label: D
options.text: Gamma rays from the glass wall cause pair production strictly at the anode.
options.distractorRationale: No gamma pair production occurs at kilovolt discharge voltages.

items.stem: Four identical point charges, each $+8.0\text{ nC}$, are placed at the four corners of a square in a vacuum. Each charge is at a distance of $8.0\text{ cm}$ from the centre P.
items.workedSolution: (a) $V_1 = \frac{8.99 \times 10^9 \times 8.0 \times 10^{-9}}{0.080} = 899 V$. (b) $V_{\text{P}} = 4 V_1 = 3.60 × 10³ V$. (c) Opposite electric field vectors cancel at P while positive scalar potentials add; replacing two opposite charges with $-8.0\text{ nC}$ gives $V_{\text{P}} = 0\text{ V}$, and equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to electric field lines and no work is done moving a charge along an equipotential. (d) Unlike the isolated zero-field point P here, a conductor has zero electric field and constant electric potential equal to the surface potential inside both solid and hollow conducting spheres.

parts.prompt: Calculate the electric potential at P due to one $+8.0\text{ nC}$ corner charge alone.
Hence calculate the total electric potential at P due to all four $+8.0\text{ nC}$ charges.
workingSteps: Multiply scalar potential by four: $V_{\text{P}} = 4 \times 899 V = 3.60 × 10³ V$.

parts.prompt: Explain why the resultant electric field strength at P is zero even though the electric potential is non-zero, and state how $V_{\text{P}}$ changes if two opposite corner charges are changed to $-8.0\text{ nC}$.
parts.expectedAnswer: Electric field is a vector so opposite corner fields cancel symmetrically to zero, whereas potential is a scalar so four positive terms sum. Replacing two opposite corners with $-8.0\text{ nC}$ makes $V_{\text{P}} = 0\text{ V}$ along nodal equipotentials; throughout, equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to electric field lines and no work is done moving a charge along an equipotential.
workingSteps: Contrast vector cancellation of equal opposite $E$ contributions with scalar addition of $V$.
Show two $+q$ and two $-q$ charges at equal distance give $V_{\text{P}} = 0$.
Relate contour geometry: equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to electric field lines and no work is done moving a charge along an equipotential.

parts.prompt: Compare the region around P in this four-charge array with the interior of a charged solid or hollow conducting sphere.
parts.expectedAnswer: In the four-charge square, $E = 0$ only at the isolated centre point P (a saddle point of $V$), whereas there is zero electric field and constant electric potential equal to the surface potential inside both solid and hollow conducting spheres throughout the entire interior volume.
workingSteps: Note that for four discrete charges, $E = 0$ holds only at the central point P and $V$ varies away from P.
Contrast with a conductor where there is zero electric field and constant electric potential equal to the surface potential inside both solid and hollow conducting spheres.
Note that zero work is needed to move a test charge anywhere inside the conducting sphere because the whole interior is one equipotential volume.

items.stem: Point charges +7 nC (left) and −2 nC (right) are fixed 0.5 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies between them, 0.3 m from +7 nC. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², with zero potential at infinity. What is the electric potential at point P?
items.workedSolution: Electric potential is a signed scalar: V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂) with r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.2 m. Thus V = 210 V + (−89.9 V) = 120 V (D).

markScheme.criterion: Sums signed scalar potentials kq₁/0.3 + kq₂/0.2 = 120 V (D).

items.stem: A parallel-plate capacitor remains permanently connected across a constant-voltage DC power supply while a polar dielectric slab of relative permittivity εᵣ is inserted between its plates. What happens to the charge and stored energy?
items.workedSolution: At fixed V, C rises by εᵣ so potential difference stays constant so extra charge flows from the supply and stored energy increases by factor relative permittivity. Therefore the correct statement is: While connected to the supply, potential difference stays constant so extra charge flows from the supply and stored energy increases by factor relative permittivity

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: potential difference stays constant so extra charge flows from the supply and stored energy increases by factor relative permittivity.

options.label: A
options.text: While connected to the supply, potential difference stays constant so extra charge flows from the supply and stored energy increases by factor relative permittivity

options.label: B
options.text: While connected to the supply, charge stays constant so potential difference and stored energy drop by factor relative permittivity.
options.distractorRationale: Applies the isolated-capacitor behaviour when V is actually held fixed by the supply.

options.label: C
options.text: While connected to the supply, capacitance stays constant so neither charge nor stored energy changes.
options.distractorRationale: Ignores that inserting a dielectric multiplies capacitance by εᵣ.

options.label: D
options.text: While connected to the supply, extra charge flows back into the battery so stored energy falls to zero.
options.distractorRationale: Higher capacitance at fixed V requires additional charge from the supply, increasing E = ½CV².

items.stem: Two fixed point charges, +9 nC on the left and −3 nC on the right, are 0.8 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.5 m from the +9 nC charge. Use 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Both individual electric field vectors at P point to the right (away from the positive left source and toward the negative right source), so they reinforce toward the right. (b) With r₁ = 0.5 m and r₂ = 0.3 m, |E₁| = 324 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = 300 N C⁻¹. Summing gives 623 N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Explains using a positive test charge that both source fields at P act in the same direction.
Applies E = k|q|/r² with r₁ = 0.5 m and r₂ = 0.3 m.
Adds the two electric field magnitudes.
Obtains 623 N C⁻¹ to the right.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude and state the direction of the resultant electric field at point P.
workingSteps: |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 324 N C⁻¹; |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 300 N C⁻¹.
Resultant E = |E₁| + |E₂| = 623 N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: Fixed point charges −8 nC (left) and −4 nC (right) are separated by 0.6 m in free space. A probe charge of +3 nC is held at point P, 0.2 m from the −8 nC charge. Use 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², with zero electric potential at infinity. Calculate the electric potential at P due to the two fixed source charges.
items.workedSolution: Electric potential at P depends only on the source charges: V = k(q₁/0.2 + q₂/0.4) = −360 V + (−89.9 V) = −450 V (B).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = k(q₁/0.2 + q₂/0.4) = −450 V (B), independent of q_test.

items.stem: Two point charges, +7 nC (left) and +5 nC (right), are fixed 0.35 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line beyond the right-hand charge, 0.7 m from +7 nC. Use the Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the resultant electric field at point P?
items.workedSolution: Exterior point P is r₁ = 0.7 m to the right of +7 nC and r₂ = 0.7 − 0.35 = 0.35 m to the right of +5 nC. Superposing E_x = kq₁/r₁² + kq₂/r₂² gives 495 N C⁻¹ to the right (B).

markScheme.criterion: Uses r₁ = 0.7 m and r₂ = 0.35 m to obtain 495 N C⁻¹ to the right (B).

items.stem: Two point charges are fixed on the x-axis in a vacuum: +4 nC at x = 0 and +9 nC at x = 0.5 m. Calculate the distance from the +4 nC charge to the point between them where the resultant electric field is zero.
items.workedSolution: Equating opposing field magnitudes gives q₁/x² = q₂/(0.5 − x)², so (0.5 − x)/x = √(9/4). Solving yields x = 0.5 × √4/(√4 + √9) = 0.200 m (D).

markScheme.criterion: Equates kq₁/x² = kq₂/(0.5 − x)² to obtain x = 0.200 m (D).

items.stem: The left-hand graph plots radial gravitational field strength g against distance r from a planet's centre, with a shaded strip between r₁ and r₂. What physical quantity is represented by the shaded area?
items.workedSolution: Units check: (N kg⁻¹) × m = J kg⁻¹, confirming that area under g–r equals the change in gravitational potential ΔV. Therefore the correct statement is: From g = −ΔV/Δr, the shaded area under the radial field strength versus distance graph between two radii equals the magnitude of the change in potential between those points.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: the shaded area under the radial field strength versus distance graph between two radii equals the magnitude of the change in potential between those points.

items.stem: A stationary calcium nucleus of charge +20e repels an alpha particle of charge +2e approaching head-on. The incoming particle comes to rest at a separation of 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and zero electric potential at infinity. What is the electric potential due to the calcium nucleus at distance r_min?
items.workedSolution: Radial potential of the +20e nucleus is V = kZe / r_min = (8.99 × 10⁹ × 20 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) / (2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 1.20 × 10⁶ V (A).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = kZe / r_min = 1.20 × 10⁶ V (A).

items.stem: Two positive point charges, +5 nC on the left and +20 nC on the right, are fixed 0.9 m apart in a vacuum. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and V = 0 at infinity. Calculate the electric potential at the point between the charges where the resultant electric field is zero.
items.workedSolution: Zero field occurs at x = 0.9 × √5/(√5 + √20) = 0.300 m from +5 nC (and 0.600 m from +20 nC). Scalar potentials add: V = k(q₁/x + q₂/(d − x)) = 450 V (C).

markScheme.criterion: Finds x = 0.300 m and sums positive scalar potentials to obtain 450 V (C).

items.stem: In a Millikan experiment ($g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $\eta = 1.81 \times 10^{-5}\text{ Pa s}$), an oil droplet ($\rho = 900\text{ kg m}^{-3}$) falls at a terminal speed of 1.40 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹. It is held stationary by 948 V across plates 14.0 mm apart.
items.workedSolution: (a) $r = 1.14 μm$. (b) $Q = 8.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ C$. (c) losing an electron decreases upward electric force so a greater balancing potential difference is required.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Stokes law with $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Correct radius 1.14 μm.
Applies $Q = 6\pi\eta r v d / V$.
Correct charge 8.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
States losing one electron reduces droplet charge and upward electric force.
Concludes a higher balancing potential difference is required to keep $QV/d = mg$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the radius of the droplet in micrometres.
Determine the initial charge on the droplet.
State and explain how the balancing voltage must change if the droplet suddenly loses one excess electron due to ionising radiation.
parts.expectedAnswer: The balancing voltage must increase because losing an electron decreases upward electric force so a greater balancing potential difference is required.
workingSteps: Loss of one electron lowers $|Q|$ from $5e$ to $4e$.
Since $QV/d = mg$ with $mg$ constant, $V$ must rise to restore equilibrium.

items.stem: A Van de Graaff dome is charged to a steady high positive potential on an insulating stand. Which statement accurately describes the electric field and potential inside the hollow metal dome?
items.workedSolution: Excess charge sits on the outer surface; E = 0 throughout the interior, so ΔV = 0 and the whole conductor is at uniform surface potential. Therefore the correct statement is: Excess charge resides entirely on the outer conducting surface so the electric field inside is zero and the entire sphere is an equipotential.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: excess charge resides entirely on the outer conducting surface so the electric field inside is zero and the entire sphere is an equipotential.

items.stem: Two fixed point charges, +6Q (left) and +27Q (right), are separated by 4 x in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 1 x to the right of +6Q. Write the magnitude of the resultant electric field at P in the form E = α kQ/x², where k is the Coulomb constant.
items.workedSolution: (a) The left positive charge produces a larger repulsive field magnitude at P than the right positive charge, so the net electric field points to the right. (b) α = |6/1² − 27/3²| = |6.00 − 3.00| = 3.00.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies resultant direction as to the right with valid reasoning.
Forms inverse-square terms 6/1² and 27/3².
Subtracts the opposing dimensionless field coefficients.
Obtains α = 3.00.

items.stem: Two point charges lie on the x-axis in a vacuum: q₁ = 5 × 10⁻⁹ C at x = 0 and an unknown charge q₂ at x = 0.9 m. The resultant electric field is zero at x = 0.3 m.
items.workedSolution: (a) q₁ and q₂ have the same sign so their fields oppose between them. (b) |q₂/q₁| = ((0.9 − 0.3)/0.3)² = (0.6/0.3)² = 4.00. (c) q₂ = +(4.00)(5 × 10⁻⁹ C) = +2.00 × 10⁻⁸ C.

markScheme.criterion: States same sign because fields must oppose in the region between the charges.
Uses |q₂/q₁| = ((d − x₀)/x₀)² with d − x₀ = 0.6 m.
Obtains 4.00.
Multiplies q₁ by ratio from (b) with positive sign.
Obtains q₂ = +2.00 × 10⁻⁸ C.

parts.expectedAnswer: They have the same sign because their individual electric field vectors must point in opposite directions to cancel between the charges.

items.stem: Equipotential contours separated by equal potential steps ΔV are drawn around a negatively charged sphere. Why are the contours packed closer together near the sphere and wider apart far away?
items.workedSolution: Since E = −ΔV/Δr (and g = −ΔV/Δr), field strength equals the negative potential gradient so more closely spaced equipotentials indicate a stronger field. Therefore the correct statement is: Because field strength equals the negative potential gradient so more closely spaced equipotentials indicate a stronger field

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: field strength equals the negative potential gradient so more closely spaced equipotentials indicate a stronger field.

items.stem: A parallel-plate capacitor remains wired across a steady 12.0 V DC power unit while a polar glass dielectric plate (εᵣ = 3.20) slides smoothly to fill the plate separation. The overlapping plate area is 240 cm², plate separation is 0.800 mm, and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) C' = 850 pF. (b) 10.2 nC. (c) E' = 61.2 nJ. (d) polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity.

markScheme.criterion: Converts cm² and mm to SI units in C = ε₀ εᵣ A / d.
Calculates C' = 850 pF.
Recognises supply holds V constant so Q' = C' V₀.
Obtains 10.2 nC.
Calculates final stored energy E' = 61.2 nJ.
States polar molecules rotate so negative ends face the positive plate.

Explains opposing internal field lowers net field and raises capacitance (polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity).

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates in a vacuum are 0.04 m apart and held at 500 V and 0 V. A proton of mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and charge +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is released from rest at the 500 V plate. Ignore gravitational and relativistic effects.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E = V / d.
Obtains 1.25 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.
Equates kinetic energy gain to electrical work qV.
Obtains 8.00 × 10⁻¹⁷ J.
Rearranges ½mv² = ΔE_k for v = √(2ΔE_k / m).
Obtains 3.10 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Two point charges are fixed on the x-axis in a vacuum: +2 nC at x = 0 and +10 nC at x = 0.6 m. Point P lies on the axis at x = 0.4 m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the resultant electric field at point P?
items.workedSolution: Between like-sign charges, the individual fields at P oppose each other: |E₁| = k|q₁|/(0.4)² = 112 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/(0.2)² = 2.25 × 10³ N C⁻¹. Subtracting gives |E_net| = 2.14 × 10³ N C⁻¹ directed to the left (A).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts opposing inverse-square field contributions to obtain 2.14 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (A).

items.stem: Two fixed point charges lie on the x-axis: −6 nC at x = 0 and +6 nC at x = 0.6 m. Point P lies between them at x = 0.3 m, where the electric potential is zero. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and V = 0 at infinity. Determine the resultant electric field at point P.
items.workedSolution: Even though V = kq₁/r₁ + kq₂/r₂ = 0 at P, the potential gradient dV/dx is non-zero because both opposite charges drive a positive test charge to the left: E = 599 N C⁻¹ + 599 N C⁻¹ = 1.20 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (B).

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes E != 0 when V = 0 and adds the field contributions along the line to obtain 1.20 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (B).

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates are 0.03 m apart in a vacuum with a potential difference of 450 V. A small charged particle of mass 3 × 10⁻⁶ kg and charge +6 × 10⁻⁹ C moves from the +450 V plate to the 0 V plate. Neglecting edge effects, calculate the uniform electric field strength between the plates.

items.stem: Three parallel vertical equipotential lines lie in a uniform electric field, spaced 0.03 m apart. From left to right, their potentials are 400 V, 250 V, and 100 V. A charged bead of mass 5 × 10⁻⁵ kg and charge +3 × 10⁻⁸ C starts from rest on the middle 250 V line. It moves horizontally without friction to the 100 V line. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the uniform electric field.
items.workedSolution: Electric field points toward decreasing potential (to the right) with magnitude E = |ΔV|/s = (250 − 100) / 0.03 = 5.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right (D).

markScheme.criterion: Uses E = −ΔV/Δx to obtain 5.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right (D).

parts.prompt: Calculate the relativistic mass ratio $m / m_0$ at $v = 0.950c$.
Calculate the total relativistic energy $E$ of one electron in MeV.
Calculate the relativistic kinetic energy of one electron in joules.

items.stem: A negatively charged insulating rod is brought close to (without touching) a neutral metal sphere on an insulating stand. The sphere is briefly connected to Earth, the Earth wire is disconnected, and finally the rod is removed. What is the role of grounding in this charging-by-induction sequence?
items.workedSolution: The negative rod repels free electrons on the sphere to Earth through the grounding wire; removing the Earth link before removing the rod traps a positive deficit of electrons, illustrating that earthing allows electrons to move between Earth and the conductor leaving a permanent opposite net charge.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that earthing allows electrons to move between Earth and the conductor leaving a permanent opposite net charge.

options.text: Grounding transfers positive nuclei from Earth onto the sphere so it acquires the same negative sign as the rod.
options.distractorRationale: Only mobile electrons move through the metal conductor and Earth lead; positive ions remain fixed in the lattice.

options.label: B
options.text: Grounding permanently neutralizes the sphere so it always ends with zero net charge after the rod is withdrawn.
options.distractorRationale: Because the Earth link is broken while the charged rod is still nearby, the repelled electrons cannot return.

options.label: C
options.text: Brief earthing allows electrons to move between Earth and the conductor leaving a permanent opposite net charge on the sphere (positive in this case) once the Earth link and rod are removed in order.

options.label: D
options.text: Grounding creates electrostatic friction that strips protons directly from the negatively charged insulating rod.
options.distractorRationale: The rod never contacts the sphere and protons do not transfer in electrostatic charging.

items.stem: Two point charges, +9 nC on the left and −3 nC on the right, are fixed 0.6 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.3 m from the +9 nC charge. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electric potential at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) Scalar potential V = k(q₁/0.3 + q₂/0.3) = 180 V. (b) Vector electric field E = 1.20 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Applies signed scalar sum V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂).
Obtains V = 180 V (including sign if negative).
Uses inverse-square magnitudes at r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.3 m.
Combines the two electric field vectors along the line with proper directions.
Obtains 1.20 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: Two point charges, +8 nC (left) and −4 nC (right), are held 0.6 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line joining them, 0.4 m to the right of the +8 nC charge. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Determine the magnitude and direction of the net electric field at point P.
items.workedSolution: At P, both opposite-sign sources drive a positive test charge to the right. |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 449 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 899 N C⁻¹ (with r₂ = 0.2 m). Summing the two same-sense vectors gives E = 1.35 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (A).

markScheme.criterion: Adds same-direction inverse-square contributions to obtain 1.35 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (A).

items.workedSolution: (a) 3.60 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹. (b) 4.50 × 10⁴ V. (c) 0.135 J. (d) field strength equals the negative gradient of the potential versus distance graph, so the steepest potential gradient occurs closest to the surface.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E = (Q/4πε₀) / r².
Obtains E₁ = 3.60 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹.
Computes ΔV = (Q/4πε₀)(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).
Obtains |ΔV| = 4.50 × 10⁴ V.
Computes ΔW = 0.135 J.
States E equals magnitude of potential gradient ΔV/Δr.
Notes the 1/r potential curve is steepest closest to the surface.

items.stem: An alpha particle of charge +2e approaches a stationary titanium nucleus head-on. The nucleus has atomic number Z = 22 (charge +22e), and the distance of closest approach is r_min = 2.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and zero electric potential at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) V = kZe / r_min = 1.22 × 10⁶ V. (b) E_p = 2eV = 3.89 × 10⁻¹³ J. (c) Dividing by e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ gives 2.43 × 10⁶ eV.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes Q = 22e and r_min = 2.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ m into V = kQ/r.
Obtains 1.22 × 10⁶ V.
Multiplies potential from (a) by projectile charge 2e.
Obtains 3.89 × 10⁻¹³ J.
Divides joule energy by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ (or multiplies V in volts by z).

items.stem: A charged Van de Graaff dome of radius R₁ stands on an insulating column. It is briefly joined by a long thin wire to an initially uncharged metal sphere of radius R₂.
items.workedSolution: Isolated sphere capacitance equals 4 pi epsilon zero R and connecting spheres conserves charge while equalising potential and dissipating electrostatic energy. Outside a charged sphere, charge acts as if concentrated at the centre so surface potential is V = Q/(4πε₀R); substituting into C = Q/V gives C = 4πε₀R. Connecting the spheres allows electrons to flow until both share the same potential V_f = Q/(C₁ + C₂) while total charge Q = Q₁' + Q₂' is conserved, so charge divides in proportion to radius (Q ∝ R). Because E_f = Q²/[2(C₁ + C₂)] < Q²/(2C₁), stored electrostatic energy decreases, with the difference dissipated as heating in the wire and EM radiation in the spark.

markScheme.criterion: L1: States surface electric potential of an isolated charged sphere is V = Q/(4πε₀R).
L1: Combines C = Q/V with V = Q/(4πε₀R) to derive C = 4πε₀R.
L2: Explains charge flows along the connecting wire until both spheres reach equal electric potential V_f.
L2: Applies conservation of total charge Q = Q₁' + Q₂' to show final charge divides proportionally to radius (Q ∝ R).
L3: Uses E = Q²/(2C) to prove total stored electrostatic energy decreases because combined capacitance C₁ + C₂ > C₁.
L3: Accounts for energy conservation via resistive thermal heating in the wire and spark/electromagnetic radiation.

Connecting the spheres allows electrons to flow until both share the same potential V_f = Q/(C₁ + C₂) while total charge Q = Q₁' + Q₂' is conserved, so charge divides in proportion to radius (Q ∝ R). Because E_f = Q²/[2(C₁ + C₂)] < Q²/(2C₁), stored electrostatic energy decreases, with the difference dissipated as heating in the wire and EM radiation in the spark.

items.stem: Two positive point charges, +6Q on the left and +9Q on the right, are fixed a distance 4 x apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 2 x from +6Q and 2 x from +9Q. Using the Coulomb constant k, express the resultant electric field at P in terms of kQ/x².
items.workedSolution: At P, +6Q produces (6/2²) kQ/x² = 1.50 kQ/x² to the right, while +9Q at distance 2 x produces (9/2²) kQ/x² = 2.25 kQ/x² to the left. Net field = 0.750 kQ/x² to the left (C).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts (6/2²) and (9/2²) to obtain 0.750 kQ/x² to the left (C).

items.stem: Which statement accurately compares radial gravitational fields around a spherical mass and radial electric fields around a point charge?
items.workedSolution: Both obey inverse-square laws with zero potential at infinity, but gravitational force is always attractive with negative potential whereas electric force can attract or repel with positive or negative potential. Therefore the correct statement is: In radial geometry, both obey inverse-square laws with zero potential at infinity, but gravitational force is always attractive with negative potential whereas electric force can attract or repel with positive or negative potential
