options.label: A
options.text: In radial geometry, gravitational field strength obeys an inverse-cube law while electric field strength obeys an inverse-square law.
options.distractorRationale: Both radial fields follow inverse-square laws (1/r²).

options.label: B
options.text: In radial geometry, gravitational potential is positive near a mass whereas electric potential is always negative near any charge.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the sign of gravitational potential and ignores positive electric potential near +Q.

options.label: C
options.text: In radial geometry, both fields can attract or repel depending on whether the test particle is moving.
options.distractorRationale: Gravity is always attractive; static electric forces depend on charge sign, not motion.

options.label: D
options.text: In radial geometry, both obey inverse-square laws with zero potential at infinity, but gravitational force is always attractive with negative potential whereas electric force can attract or repel with positive or negative potential

items.stem: While permanently connected to a 30.0 V laboratory supply, a parallel-plate capacitor has its air gap filled completely with a polar ceramic dielectric (εᵣ = 5.50). The overlapping plate area is 350 cm², plate separation is 1.50 mm, and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) C' = 1.14 × 10³ pF. (b) 34.1 nC. (c) E' = 511 nJ. (d) polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity.

markScheme.criterion: Converts cm² and mm to SI units in C = ε₀ εᵣ A / d.
Calculates C' = 1.14 × 10³ pF.
Recognises supply holds V constant so Q' = C' V₀.
Obtains 34.1 nC.
Calculates final stored energy E' = 511 nJ.
States polar molecules rotate so negative ends face the positive plate.

Explains opposing internal field lowers net field and raises capacitance (polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity).

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates in a vacuum are 0.04 m apart, with a potential difference of 500 V between them. A proton of charge +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg starts from rest at the positive plate and accelerates to the 0 V plate. Neglecting gravity, calculate the speed of the proton when it reaches the 0 V plate.
items.workedSolution: By conservation of energy, ½mv² = qV, so v = √(2qV / m) = √(2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 500 / 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷) = 3.10 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (A).

markScheme.criterion: Equates ½mv² = qV to obtain v = 3.10 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: Two point charges, +10 nC on the left and +4 nC on the right, are fixed 0.9 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies between them, 0.3 m from the left charge. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Both positive sources repel a positive test charge placed at P, so the left charge pushes rightward while the right charge pushes leftward. (b) |E₁| = k|q₁|/(0.3)² = 999 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/(0.6)² = 99.9 N C⁻¹. Subtracting the opposing vectors yields 899 N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: States that a positive test charge between like-sign sources experiences opposite forces from the left and right charges.
Evaluates E = k|q|/r² at r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.6 m.
Subtracts the two opposing field magnitudes.
Obtains 899 N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.workedSolution: (a) E = (320 − 100) / 0.055 = 4.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right. (b) a = qE / m = 20.0 m s⁻². (c) Using ½mv² = q(220), v = 1.48 m s⁻¹.

Obtains 20.0 m s⁻².

Obtains 1.48 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: An isolated conducting sphere of radius $R = 10.0\text{ cm}$ in vacuum carries a charge of $+40.0\text{ nC}$. A test point A lies outside the sphere at a radial distance $r = 25.0\text{ cm}$ from the centre.
items.workedSolution: (a) Inside the conductor $E = 0$, so $V = kQ/R = 3.60 × 10³ V$. (b) At $r = 0.250\text{ m}$, $E = kQ/r^2 = 5.75 × 10³ N C⁻¹$. (c) $V = kQ/r = 1.44 × 10³ V$. (d) In electrostatic equilibrium all excess charge sits on the outer surface, yielding zero electric field and constant electric potential equal to the surface potential inside both solid and hollow conducting spheres.

markScheme.criterion: Uses surface radius $R = 0.100\text{ m}$ in $V = kQ/R$ because interior potential is constant.
Correct interior potential 3.60 × 10³ V.
Applies $E = kQ/r^2$ with $r = 0.250\text{ m}$.
Correct field strength 5.75 × 10³ N C⁻¹.
Correct exterior potential 1.44 × 10³ V.
States excess charge sits only on the outer surface in both solid and hollow conductors.
Explains zero electric field and constant electric potential equal to the surface potential inside both solid and hollow conducting spheres.

parts.prompt: Calculate the electric potential at a point $4.0\text{ cm}$ from the centre inside the conducting sphere.
workingSteps: Inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, $E = 0$ so potential equals the surface potential $V = kQ/R$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the electric field strength at point A ($r = 25.0\text{ cm}$) outside the sphere.
workingSteps: Outside the sphere, the field behaves as if all charge were at the centre: $E = kQ/r^2$.
Substitute $r = 0.250\text{ m}$ to obtain $E = 5.75 × 10³ N C⁻¹$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the electric potential at point A ($r = 25.0\text{ cm}$).
Explain why the electric field strength and potential inside the sphere would remain identical if the solid metal sphere were replaced by a hollow conducting shell of the same radius and charge.
parts.expectedAnswer: Mutual repulsion forces all excess charge only onto the outer conducting surface, producing zero electric field and constant electric potential equal to the surface potential inside both solid and hollow conducting spheres.
workingSteps: State that free charges migrate until all excess charge resides on the outer surface.
Link $E = -\Delta V_{\text{e}}/\Delta r = 0$ to zero electric field and constant electric potential equal to the surface potential inside both solid and hollow conducting spheres.

items.stem: Two fixed point charges of +12 nC (left) and −5 nC (right) are separated by 0.8 m in a vacuum. Point P is on the line joining them, 0.3 m from the +12 nC charge. Assume a vacuum with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero potential at infinity. Determine the electric potential at point P.
items.workedSolution: Electric potential is a signed scalar: V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂) with r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.5 m. Thus V = 360 V + (−89.9 V) = 270 V (B).

markScheme.criterion: Sums signed scalar potentials kq₁/0.3 + kq₂/0.5 = 270 V (B).

items.stem: An air-filled capacitor (area 400 cm², gap 1.00 mm, ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹) is charged to 40.0 V and then disconnected. A dielectric slab with εᵣ = 4.00 is inserted to fill the gap. Calculate the final electrical energy stored in nanojoules.
items.workedSolution: C₀ = 354 pF, E₀ = ½C₀V₀² = 283 nJ. Isolated Q fixed ⇒ E' = E₀ / εᵣ = 70.8 nJ.

markScheme.criterion: Finds isolated final energy 70.8 nJ.

items.stem: Two point charges of +3.5 nC and −7 nC are fixed 0.7 m apart on a horizontal line, with +3.5 nC on the left. Point P lies between them, 0.2 m from the left charge. Use the Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Both individual electric field vectors at P point to the right (away from the positive left source and toward the negative right source), so they reinforce toward the right. (b) With r₁ = 0.2 m and r₂ = 0.5 m, |E₁| = 787 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = 252 N C⁻¹. Summing gives 1.04 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Explains using a positive test charge that both source fields at P act in the same direction.
Applies E = k|q|/r² with r₁ = 0.2 m and r₂ = 0.5 m.
Adds the two electric field magnitudes.
Obtains 1.04 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

parts.expectedAnswer: Both individual electric field vectors at P point to the right (away from the positive left source and toward the negative right source), so they reinforce toward the right.
workingSteps: Electric field direction is the force direction on a positive test charge.
Both individual electric field vectors at P point to the right (away from the positive left source and toward the negative right source), so they reinforce toward the right.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude and state the direction of the resultant electric field at point P.
workingSteps: |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 787 N C⁻¹; |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 252 N C⁻¹.
Resultant E = |E₁| + |E₂| = 1.04 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: Two point charges, −4 nC on the left and +10 nC on the right, are fixed 0.6 m apart in a vacuum. A small test charge of −2.5 nC is placed at point P, 0.4 m from −4 nC. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electric potential at infinity. Calculate the electric potential at P due to the two fixed source charges.
items.workedSolution: Electric potential at P depends only on the source charges: V = k(q₁/0.4 + q₂/0.2) = −89.9 V + (450 V) = 360 V (D).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = k(q₁/0.4 + q₂/0.2) = 360 V (D), independent of q_test.

items.stem: Point charges −14 nC and +3 nC are fixed 0.6 m apart on a horizontal line, with −14 nC on the left. Point P lies on the same line, 0.9 m to the right of −14 nC. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the resultant electric field at point P?
items.workedSolution: Exterior point P is r₁ = 0.9 m to the right of −14 nC and r₂ = 0.9 − 0.6 = 0.3 m to the right of +3 nC. Superposing E_x = kq₁/r₁² + kq₂/r₂² gives 144 N C⁻¹ to the right (A).

markScheme.criterion: Uses r₁ = 0.9 m and r₂ = 0.3 m to obtain 144 N C⁻¹ to the right (A).

items.stem: Two point charges are fixed on the x-axis in a vacuum: +9 nC at x = 0 and +16 nC at x = 0.7 m. Calculate the distance from the +9 nC charge to the point between them where the resultant electric field is zero.
items.workedSolution: Equating opposing field magnitudes gives q₁/x² = q₂/(0.7 − x)², so (0.7 − x)/x = √(16/9). Solving yields x = 0.7 × √9/(√9 + √16) = 0.300 m (B).

markScheme.criterion: Equates kq₁/x² = kq₂/(0.7 − x)² to obtain x = 0.300 m (B).

options.distractorRationale: Proportions the distance linearly with charge q₁/(q₁ + q₂) instead of using square roots √q₁/(√q₁ + √q₂) from the inverse-square law.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the distance of the null point from the right-hand charge rather than from the left-hand charge.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Assumes the electric fields cancel at the geometric midpoint despite the unequal source magnitudes.

items.stem: Two stationary point charges, +7 nC (left) and −4 nC (right), are held 0.6 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.3 m from the left charge. A small test charge of +4 nC is placed at P without moving the fixed charges. Use the Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Calculate the resultant electric force on the +4 nC test charge.
items.workedSolution: At P (r₁ = 0.3 m, r₂ = 0.3 m), the resultant electric field is E = 1.10 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right. Multiplying by q_test = +4 nC gives F = q_test E = 4.40 × 10⁻⁶ N to the right (A).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates E = 1.10 × 10³ N C⁻¹ and F = qE = 4.40 × 10⁻⁶ N to the right (A).

items.stem: A student estimates the shaded area under the radial g–r graph between r₁ and r₂ using one trapezium joining (r₁, g₁) and (r₂, g₂), as shown by the dashed chord. How does this estimate compare with the exact value of |ΔV|?
items.workedSolution: Since d²g/dr² = 6GM/r⁴ > 0, the g–r curve is concave up, placing any straight chord slightly above the true curve. Therefore the correct statement is: Because g is proportional to 1/r², a single trapezium chord lies above the concave-up inverse-square curve, so it slightly overestimates the true area and exact change in potential.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: a single trapezium chord lies above the concave-up inverse-square curve, so it slightly overestimates the true area and exact change in potential.

options.label: A
options.text: A single trapezium gives the exact value of ΔV because the inverse-square curvature cancels symmetrically about the midpoint.
options.distractorRationale: Only a linear function has exact single-trapezium area; 1/r² curves upward.

options.label: B
options.text: A single trapezium underestimates ΔV because the curve bows upward above the straight chord joining its endpoints.
options.distractorRationale: An inverse-square decay curve bows downward below the straight chord, so the chord encloses extra area above the curve.

options.label: C
options.text: Because g is proportional to 1/r², a single trapezium chord lies above the concave-up inverse-square curve, so it slightly overestimates the true area and exact change in potential.

options.label: D
options.text: A single trapezium can only estimate Δg and cannot be improved by subdividing into narrower strips.
options.distractorRationale: Using narrower trapezium strips or counting fine grid squares converges closely to exact |ΔV|.

items.stem: Three parallel equipotential lines lie in a uniform electric field, spaced 0.06 m apart. From left to right, their potentials are 60 V, -60 V, and -180 V. A particle of charge −1.5 × 10⁻⁸ C moves from the 60 V line to the -180 V line.

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE_p = q(V_final − V_initial) with ΔV = -240 V.
Obtains ΔE_p = 3.60 × 10⁻⁶ J (with correct sign).
Applies W_field = −ΔE_p = q(V_initial − V_final).
Obtains W_field = −3.60 × 10⁻⁶ J (with correct sign).

items.stem: An alpha particle of charge +2e approaches a stationary iron nucleus of charge +26e head-on. Their minimum centre-to-centre separation is 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and zero electric potential at infinity. Calculate the electrostatic potential energy of the system at closest approach, in electronvolts (eV).
items.workedSolution: At r_min, V = kZe / r_min = 1.17 × 10⁶ V. For a +2e projectile, E_p = 2eV = 2.34 × 10⁶ eV (D).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = 1.17 × 10⁶ V and E_p = 2V (in eV) = 2.34 × 10⁶ eV (D).

parts.prompt: Calculate the weight of the oil droplet.
Calculate the charge $Q$ on the droplet.
Explain how repeating this calculation for many droplets led to the concept of charge quantisation.
parts.expectedAnswer: Millikan found that all measured droplet charges are integer multiples of the elementary charge proving charge is quantised, never smaller fractions of $1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$.
workingSteps: Every measured droplet charge was a whole-number multiple of $1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$.
Hence charge exists in discrete packets of the elementary charge $e$.

items.stem: When a charged isolated conducting sphere is connected by a thin wire to an initially uncharged conducting sphere, total charge is conserved. What happens to the total stored electrostatic energy?
items.workedSolution: At fixed total charge Q, increasing total capacitance from C₁ to C₁ + C₂ lowers E = Q²/(2C), dissipating ΔE as heat in the wire and EM radiation. Therefore the correct statement is: Total stored electrostatic energy decreases during charge sharing because energy is dissipated as thermal heating in the connecting wire and electromagnetic radiation.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: total stored electrostatic energy decreases during charge sharing because energy is dissipated as thermal heating in the connecting wire and electromagnetic radiation.

items.stem: Two fixed point charges, +5Q (left) and +18Q (right), are separated by 4 x in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 1 x to the right of +5Q. Write the magnitude of the resultant electric field at P in the form E = α kQ/x², where k is the Coulomb constant.
items.workedSolution: (a) The left positive charge produces a larger repulsive field magnitude at P than the right positive charge, so the net electric field points to the right. (b) α = |5/1² − 18/3²| = |5.00 − 2.00| = 3.00.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies resultant direction as to the right with valid reasoning.
Forms inverse-square terms 5/1² and 18/3².
Subtracts the opposing dimensionless field coefficients.
Obtains α = 3.00.

items.stem: Two point charges lie on the x-axis in a vacuum: q₁ = 9 × 10⁻⁹ C at x = 0 and an unknown charge q₂ at x = 0.6 m. The resultant electric field is zero at x = 0.36 m.
items.workedSolution: (a) q₁ and q₂ have the same sign so their fields oppose between them. (b) |q₂/q₁| = ((0.6 − 0.36)/0.36)² = (0.24/0.36)² = 0.444. (c) q₂ = +(0.444)(9 × 10⁻⁹ C) = +4.00 × 10⁻⁹ C.

markScheme.criterion: States same sign because fields must oppose in the region between the charges.
Uses |q₂/q₁| = ((d − x₀)/x₀)² with d − x₀ = 0.24 m.
Obtains 0.444.
Multiplies q₁ by ratio from (b) with positive sign.
Obtains q₂ = +4.00 × 10⁻⁹ C.

parts.prompt: State whether q₁ and q₂ have the same sign or opposite signs, explaining your reasoning.
parts.expectedAnswer: They have the same sign because their individual electric field vectors must point in opposite directions to cancel between the charges.
workingSteps: Opposite-sign charges produce fields in the same direction everywhere between them.
Therefore q₁ and q₂ must have the same sign.

parts.prompt: Calculate the ratio |q₂ / q₁|.
workingSteps: Distance from q₂ to null point = 0.6 − 0.36 = 0.24 m.

parts.prompt: Hence determine the signed value of q₂.
workingSteps: q₂ is positive (same sign as q₁) with magnitude 0.444 × 9 × 10⁻⁹ C.

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates in a vacuum are 0.06 m apart, with a potential difference of 2400 V between them. A singly charged ion of argon of charge +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and mass 6.63 × 10⁻²⁶ kg starts from rest at the positive plate and accelerates to the 0 V plate. Ignore gravitational and relativistic effects.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E = V / d.
Obtains 4.00 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.
Equates kinetic energy gain to electrical work qV.
Obtains 3.84 × 10⁻¹⁶ J.
Rearranges ½mv² = ΔE_k for v = √(2ΔE_k / m).
Obtains 1.08 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the electric field between the plates.
Determine the kinetic energy gained by the singly charged ion of argon on reaching the 0 V plate.
Hence calculate the speed of the singly charged ion of argon as it reaches the 0 V plate.

items.stem: Two point charges, +6 nC (left) and +2 nC (right), are held 0.4 m apart along a straight line. Point P lies between them, 0.15 m from the +6 nC charge. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Calculate the magnitude and direction of the resultant electric field at point P.
items.workedSolution: Between like-sign charges, the individual fields at P oppose each other: |E₁| = k|q₁|/(0.15)² = 2.40 × 10³ N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/(0.25)² = 288 N C⁻¹. Subtracting gives |E_net| = 2.11 × 10³ N C⁻¹ directed to the right (D).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts opposing inverse-square field contributions to obtain 2.11 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (D).

items.stem: Two opposite point charges, −9 nC on the left and +3 nC on the right, are separated by 0.8 m. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.6 m from −9 nC. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electric potential at infinity. The electric potential at P is zero. Calculate the resultant electric field at P.
items.workedSolution: Even though V = kq₁/r₁ + kq₂/r₂ = 0 at P, the potential gradient dV/dx is non-zero because both opposite charges drive a positive test charge to the left: E = 225 N C⁻¹ + 674 N C⁻¹ = 899 N C⁻¹ to the left (C).

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes E != 0 when V = 0 and adds the field contributions along the line to obtain 899 N C⁻¹ to the left (C).

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates are 0.04 m apart with a potential difference of 320 V (from 320 V on the left plate to 0 V on the right plate). A positively charged droplet of charge +8 × 10⁻⁹ C and mass 4 × 10⁻⁶ kg is released at the 320 V plate. Ignore edge effects. Calculate the magnitude of the uniform electric field between the plates.
items.workedSolution: For uniform parallel plates, E = V / d = 320 / 0.04 = 8.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ (C).

A charged bead (m = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ kg, q = +2.5 × 10⁻⁸ C) is released from rest on the middle 180 V line. It accelerates horizontally across one spacing to the 60 V line. Calculate the magnitude of the horizontal electric acceleration of the charged bead.

markScheme.criterion: Finds E = 3.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ and a = qE/m = 5.00 m s⁻² (C).

items.stem: A cold-cathode gas-discharge tube containing neon at low pressure is connected to a $5.40\text{ kV}$ DC supply. A bright glow appears in the tube and cathode rays pass through a hole in the anode.
items.workedSolution: (a) High pd ionises gas so positive gas ions accelerate into the cold cathode knocking out electrons as cathode rays. (b) electrons collide with and excite gas atoms which emit visible photons on de-excitation, whereas thermionic emission heats a cathode filament in a vacuum. (c) $v = \sqrt{2eV/m_{\text{e}}} = 4.36 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: High pd ionises low-pressure gas atoms into positive ions and electrons.
Explains positive gas ions accelerate into the cold cathode knocking out electrons as cathode rays.
Explains electrons collide with and excite gas atoms which emit visible photons on de-excitation.
Contrasts cold-cathode gas ion bombardment with heated-filament thermionic emission.
Substitutes $V = 5400\text{ V}$ into $v = \sqrt{2eV/m_{\text{e}}}$.

parts.prompt: Explain how cathode rays are produced inside this cold-cathode gas-discharge tube.
parts.expectedAnswer: The high potential difference ionises some gas atoms, and positive gas ions accelerate into the cold cathode knocking out electrons as cathode rays toward the anode.
workingSteps: High pd ionises residual gas molecules creating electrons and positive ions.
State positive gas ions accelerate into the cold cathode knocking out electrons as cathode rays.

parts.prompt: Explain why the gas in the tube emits visible light and contrast this cold-cathode process with thermionic emission.
parts.expectedAnswer: Fast electrons collide with and excite gas atoms which emit visible photons on de-excitation; unlike a thermionic tube (which boils electrons from a hot filament in a hard vacuum), this cold-cathode tube relies on residual low-pressure gas ionisation.
workingSteps: State electrons collide with and excite gas atoms which emit visible photons on de-excitation.
Contrast cold-cathode ion bombardment in low-pressure gas with heated-filament thermionic emission in vacuum.

items.stem: Four identical point charges, each of $+6.0\text{ nC}$, are fixed at the four corners of a square in a vacuum. Each corner lies at a distance of $10.0\text{ cm}$ from the geometric centre P of the square. What is the total electric potential at P?
items.workedSolution: Electric potential is a scalar quantity, so the four equal contributions add directly: $V_{\text{P}} = 4 \times \frac{k q}{r} = 4 \times \frac{8.99 \times 10^9 \times 6.0 \times 10^{-9}}{0.100} = 2.16 × 10³ V$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 2.16 × 10³ V.

Combines the two electric field vectors along the line with proper directions.

items.stem: An empty air-filled parallel-plate capacitor (area 500 cm², separation 0.500 mm, ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹) is charged through a 22 kΩ resistor from a constant 60.0 V supply. How much thermal energy (in nanojoules) is dissipated in the circuit resistance during complete charging?
items.workedSolution: C₀ = ε₀A/d = 885 pF. Half of battery work QV is dissipated as heat: E_heat = ½C₀V² = 1.59 × 10³ nJ.

markScheme.criterion: Applies 50% charging loss E_heat = ½C₀V² = 1.59 × 10³ nJ.

items.stem: Two point charges of +4 nC and −12 nC are fixed 0.8 m apart on a horizontal line, with +4 nC on the left. Point P lies between them, 0.3 m from the left charge. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the resultant electric field at point P?
items.workedSolution: At P, both opposite-sign sources drive a positive test charge to the right. |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 400 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 432 N C⁻¹ (with r₂ = 0.5 m). Summing the two same-sense vectors gives E = 831 N C⁻¹ to the right (A).

markScheme.criterion: Adds same-direction inverse-square contributions to obtain 831 N C⁻¹ to the right (A).

parts.prompt: Calculate the distance from the +20 nC charge to the point X between the charges where the resultant electric field is zero.
Calculate the electric potential at point X.
State the magnitude of the resultant electric field at X even though the potential there is non-zero.
workingSteps: At point X the potential has a local spatial extremum (dV/dx = 0), so E = 0 N C⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 948 V.

items.stem: An isolated conducting sphere of radius 16.0 cm is charged to 25.0 kV ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F m}^{-1}$). It is later connected via switch S and a long thin wire to an initially uncharged metal sphere of radius 8.00 cm.
items.workedSolution: (a) C₁ = 17.8 pF. (b) E₁ = 5.56 mJ. (c) V_f = 16.7 kV. (d) total stored electrostatic energy decreases during charge sharing because energy is dissipated as thermal heating in the connecting wire and electromagnetic radiation.

markScheme.criterion: Converts radius to metres and applies C = 4πε₀R.
Obtains C₁ = 17.8 pF.
Applies E = ½CV² (or Q²/(8πε₀R)).
Obtains E₁ = 5.56 mJ.
Applies charge conservation Q = (C₁ + C₂)V_f with C ∝ R.
Obtains common potential V_f = 16.7 kV.
Notes total capacitance increases at fixed Q so E = Q²/(2C) drops.

Explains transfer to heat in wire and EM radiation (total stored electrostatic energy decreases during charge sharing because energy is dissipated as thermal heating in the connecting wire and electromagnetic radiation).

parts.prompt: Using $C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 R$, calculate the capacitance $C_1$ of sphere 1 in picofarads.
Calculate the electrostatic energy stored on sphere 1 before closing switch S, in millijoules.
Switch S is closed so the two spheres share charge until equilibrium. Calculate their final common potential in kilovolts.
Explain why the total electrostatic energy stored on both spheres after closing S is less than your answer to part (b).
parts.expectedAnswer: Energy is not retained electrostatically because total stored electrostatic energy decreases during charge sharing because energy is dissipated as thermal heating in the connecting wire and electromagnetic radiation.
workingSteps: total stored electrostatic energy decreases during charge sharing because energy is dissipated as thermal heating in the connecting wire and electromagnetic radiation.

items.stem: Two fixed point charges, +7Q (left) and +8Q (right), are separated by 3 x in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 1 x to the right of +7Q. Using the Coulomb constant k, express the resultant electric field at P in terms of kQ/x².
items.workedSolution: At P, +7Q produces (7/1²) kQ/x² = 7.00 kQ/x² to the right, while +8Q at distance 2 x produces (8/2²) kQ/x² = 2.00 kQ/x² to the left. Net field = 5.00 kQ/x² to the right (B).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts (7/1²) and (8/2²) to obtain 5.00 kQ/x² to the right (B).

items.stem: Two fixed point charges, q₁ and q₂, are 0.9 m apart in a vacuum, with q₁ = 5 × 10⁻⁹ C on the left. The resultant electric field is zero at a point between them, 0.3 m from q₁. Calculate the signed value of charge q₂.
items.workedSolution: An interior null point requires q₁ and q₂ to have the same sign (+). Equating kq₁/x₀² = kq₂/(d − x₀)² with d − x₀ = 0.6 m gives q₂ = q₁((0.6)/(0.3))² = 4.00 × 5 × 10⁻⁹ C = +2.00 × 10⁻⁸ C (C).

markScheme.criterion: Uses q₂ = q₁((d − x₀)/x₀)² with positive sign to obtain +2.00 × 10⁻⁸ C (C).

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates in a vacuum are separated by 0.03 m and held at +900 V and 0 V. A singly charged lithium ion (charge +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass 1.16 × 10⁻²⁶ kg) starts from rest at the positive plate and accelerates to the earthed plate. Neglecting gravity, calculate the speed of the singly charged lithium ion when it reaches the 0 V plate.
items.workedSolution: By conservation of energy, ½mv² = qV, so v = √(2qV / m) = √(2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 900 / 1.16 × 10⁻²⁶) = 1.58 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (D).

markScheme.criterion: Equates ½mv² = qV to obtain v = 1.58 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: Using the exact AQA Data Sheet electron rest energy $m_0 c^2 = 0.511\text{ MeV}$ ($0.510999\text{ MeV}$), calculate the total relativistic energy $E = \frac{m_0 c^2}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}$ of an electron travelling at $v = 0.866c$.
items.workedSolution: $\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.866^2}} = 2.00$. Total energy $E = \gamma m_0 c^2 = 2.00 \times 0.511\text{ MeV} = 1.02 MeV$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 1.02 MeV.

items.stem: Two oppositely charged parallel metal plates separated by $30.0\text{ mm}$ have a potential difference of $1200\text{ V}$ between them, as shown in the field and equipotential diagram.
items.workedSolution: (a) $E = \frac{V}{d} = \frac{1200}{3.00 \times 10^{-2}} = 4.00 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹$. (b) At the plate boundaries, electric field lines bulge outward and spread apart near the plate edges showing a weaker non-uniform field. (c) Since $W = q\Delta V_{\text{e}}$, equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to electric field lines and no work is done moving a charge along an equipotential.

Describe how the electric field near the outer edges differs from the central region, referring to the diagram.
parts.expectedAnswer: Near the edges, electric field lines bulge outward and spread apart near the plate edges showing a weaker non-uniform field because the field line density decreases.
workingSteps: Point out outward curvature of field lines near the ends of the plates.
Relate wider spacing to weaker field: electric field lines bulge outward and spread apart near the plate edges showing a weaker non-uniform field.

parts.prompt: Explain why equipotential surfaces always meet electric field lines at right angles and state the work done when moving a charge along a single equipotential.
parts.expectedAnswer: Because equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to electric field lines and no work is done moving a charge along an equipotential; if any field component lay along the surface, work $W = q\Delta V_{\text{e}}$ would be non-zero, contradicting constant potential.
workingSteps: Use $W = q\Delta V_{\text{e}} = 0$ along an equipotential surface.
Conclude equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to electric field lines and no work is done moving a charge along an equipotential.

items.stem: Two fixed point charges of −9 nC (left) and +5 nC (right) are separated by 0.6 m in free space. Point P is located 0.2 m from the left-hand charge. Use 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², with zero electric potential at infinity. Determine the electric potential at point P.
items.workedSolution: Electric potential is a signed scalar: V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂) with r₁ = 0.2 m and r₂ = 0.4 m. Thus V = −405 V + (112 V) = −292 V (A).

markScheme.criterion: Sums signed scalar potentials kq₁/0.2 + kq₂/0.4 = −292 V (A).

items.stem: A parallel-plate capacitor (area 250 cm², gap 0.500 mm, ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹) stays connected to a 20.0 V supply while a dielectric slab (εᵣ = 5.00) is slid fully between its plates. Calculate the final energy stored in nanojoules.
items.workedSolution: C' = ε₀εᵣA/d = 2.21 × 10³ pF. At constant V = 20.0 V, E' = ½C'V² = 443 nJ.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates stored energy 443 nJ.

items.workedSolution: (a) Both individual electric field vectors at P point to the left (toward the negative left source and away from the positive right source), so they reinforce toward the left. (b) With r₁ = 0.4 m and r₂ = 0.5 m, |E₁| = 253 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = 324 N C⁻¹. Summing gives 576 N C⁻¹ to the left.

Applies E = k|q|/r² with r₁ = 0.4 m and r₂ = 0.5 m.
Adds the two electric field magnitudes.
Obtains 576 N C⁻¹ to the left.

workingSteps: |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 253 N C⁻¹; |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 324 N C⁻¹.

items.stem: Point charges +12 nC at x = 0 and −5 nC at x = 0.8 m are fixed in a vacuum. A probe charge of −2 nC is placed at x = 0.3 m (point P). Assume a vacuum with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero potential at infinity. Calculate the electric potential at P due to the two fixed source charges.
items.workedSolution: Electric potential at P depends only on the source charges: V = k(q₁/0.3 + q₂/0.5) = 360 V + (−89.9 V) = 270 V (A).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = k(q₁/0.3 + q₂/0.5) = 270 V (A), independent of q_test.

items.stem: Two point charges are fixed on the x-axis in a vacuum: +18 nC at x = 0 and −5 nC at x = 0.6 m. Point P lies to the right of both charges at x = 1 m (0.4 m to the right of −5 nC). Take 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Determine the resultant electric field at point P.
items.workedSolution: Exterior point P is r₁ = 1 m to the right of +18 nC and r₂ = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4 m to the right of −5 nC. Superposing E_x = kq₁/r₁² + kq₂/r₂² gives 119 N C⁻¹ to the left (C).

markScheme.criterion: Uses r₁ = 1 m and r₂ = 0.4 m to obtain 119 N C⁻¹ to the left (C).

items.stem: Two point charges, +1 nC on the left and +4 nC on the right, are fixed 0.6 m apart in a vacuum. Calculate the distance x from the +1 nC charge to the point between them where the electric field is zero.
items.workedSolution: Equating opposing field magnitudes gives q₁/x² = q₂/(0.6 − x)², so (0.6 − x)/x = √(4/1). Solving yields x = 0.6 × √1/(√1 + √4) = 0.200 m (A).

markScheme.criterion: Equates kq₁/x² = kq₂/(0.6 − x)² to obtain x = 0.200 m (A).

items.stem: Two fixed point charges of +3 nC (left) and −9 nC (right) are 0.6 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line joining them, 0.3 m from the left charge. A small test charge of +2.5 nC is placed at P without moving the fixed charges. Take 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Calculate the resultant electric force on the +2.5 nC test charge.
items.workedSolution: At P (r₁ = 0.3 m, r₂ = 0.3 m), the resultant electric field is E = 1.20 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right. Multiplying by q_test = +2.5 nC gives F = q_test E = 3.00 × 10⁻⁶ N to the right (D).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates E = 1.20 × 10³ N C⁻¹ and F = qE = 3.00 × 10⁻⁶ N to the right (D).

items.stem: A stationary aluminium nucleus of charge +13e repels an alpha particle of charge +2e approaching head-on. The incoming particle comes to rest at a separation of 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and zero electric potential at infinity. Calculate the electrostatic potential energy of the system at closest approach, in electronvolts (eV).
items.workedSolution: At r_min, V = kZe / r_min = 7.48 × 10⁵ V. For a +2e projectile, E_p = 2eV = 1.50 × 10⁶ eV (C).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = 7.48 × 10⁵ V and E_p = 2V (in eV) = 1.50 × 10⁶ eV (C).

items.stem: Two positive point charges, +3 nC on the left and +12 nC on the right, are fixed 0.75 m apart in a vacuum. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electric potential at infinity. Calculate the electric potential at the point between the charges where the resultant electric field is zero.
items.workedSolution: Zero field occurs at x = 0.75 × √3/(√3 + √12) = 0.250 m from +3 nC (and 0.500 m from +12 nC). Scalar potentials add: V = k(q₁/x + q₂/(d − x)) = 324 V (D).

markScheme.criterion: Finds x = 0.250 m and sums positive scalar potentials to obtain 324 V (D).

items.stem: Millikan's oil-drop experiment gave the first direct measurement of the elementary charge $e$. Combined with Thomson's measurement of $e/m$, this gave the mass of the electron.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 synthesis: terminal velocity with field off yields droplet radius via Stokes law and balancing the stationary droplet with electric field reveals quantised charge; covers apparatus, Stage 1 Stokes radius derivation, explicit physical assumptions, Stage 2 $QV/d = mg$, and charge quantisation.

markScheme.criterion: Describes experimental arrangement (sprayed oil droplets between parallel plates separation $d$, illuminated and timed via calibrated microscope).
Explains Stage 1 (field off): measuring constant terminal velocity $v$ and equating $6\pi\eta r v = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho g$ to deduce $r$ and $m$.
States explicit physical assumptions: spherical droplet, laminar airflow, and negligible upthrust from air.
Explains Stage 2 (field on): adjusting $V$ to hold the droplet stationary and applying $QV/d = mg$ to compute $Q$.
Explains quantisation conclusion: all measured charges and ionisation steps are integer multiples of $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$.
Notes combining Millikan's $e$ with Thomson's $e/m$ determined the electron rest mass $m_e$.

parts.prompt: Describe the experimental procedure, measurements, physical assumptions, and equations used in Millikan's oil-drop experiment to determine a droplet's charge, and explain the significance of repeating the measurement across many droplets.
parts.expectedAnswer: Millikan's experiment uses a two-stage force balance in which terminal velocity with field off yields droplet radius via Stokes law and balancing the stationary droplet with electric field reveals quantised charge. Fine oil droplets sprayed from an atomiser become charged by friction and enter a chamber between horizontal parallel plates of measured separation $d$, illuminated from the side and viewed through a travelling microscope with a calibrated graticule. In Stage 1 (electric field off), a droplet falls at constant terminal velocity $v$ (measured by timing its passage across graticule divisions). Assuming the droplet is spherical, moves slowly in laminar airflow, and air upthrust is negligible, viscous Stokes drag balances weight: $6\pi\eta r v = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho g$, which yields droplet radius $r = \sqrt{9\eta v / (2\rho g)}$ and hence mass $m = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho$. In Stage 2 (electric field on), the plate potential difference $V$ is adjusted until the droplet hovers completely stationary, where upward electrostatic force equals weight: $QV/d = mg$, giving $Q = mgd/V$. Repeating this across hundreds of droplets revealed that every measured charge—and every step change after X-ray ionisation—was an integer multiple of $1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, proving that electric charge is quantised and enabling calculation of electron mass $m_e$ from Thomson's $e/m$.
workingSteps: Describe apparatus: atomiser, parallel plates separation $d$, variable DC supply $V$, illumination, and calibrated microscope.
Stage 1 (field off): time constant terminal fall speed $v$ across known vertical distance.
Apply Stokes' law $6\pi\eta r v = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho g$ to derive radius $r$ and mass $m$.
State key assumptions: spherical droplet, slow laminar flow, negligible air upthrust.
Stage 2 (field on): adjust $V$ to hold droplet stationary so $QV/d = mg$ gives $Q = mgd/V$.
Explain significance: all charges are integer multiples of $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$ (charge quantisation) and determine $m_e$ via Thomson's $e/m$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies V_f = V₁ R₁ / (R₁ + R₂) to obtain 18.0 kV.

items.stem: Two point charges, +7Q on the left and +4Q on the right, are fixed a distance 3 x apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 2 x from the left charge. Write the magnitude of the resultant electric field at P in the form E = α kQ/x², where k is the Coulomb constant.
items.workedSolution: (a) The right positive charge produces a larger repulsive field magnitude at P than the left positive charge, so the net electric field points to the left. (b) α = |7/2² − 4/1²| = |1.75 − 4.00| = 2.25.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies resultant direction as to the left with valid reasoning.
Forms inverse-square terms 7/2² and 4/1².
Subtracts the opposing dimensionless field coefficients.
Obtains α = 2.25.

items.stem: Point charges q₁ = 2 × 10⁻⁹ C (left) and q₂ (right) are fixed 1 m apart in a vacuum. The resultant electric field is zero at a point between them, 0.2 m to the right of q₁.
items.workedSolution: (a) q₁ and q₂ have the same sign so their fields oppose between them. (b) |q₂/q₁| = ((1 − 0.2)/0.2)² = (0.8/0.2)² = 16.0. (c) q₂ = +(16.0)(2 × 10⁻⁹ C) = +3.20 × 10⁻⁸ C.

markScheme.criterion: States same sign because fields must oppose in the region between the charges.
Uses |q₂/q₁| = ((d − x₀)/x₀)² with d − x₀ = 0.8 m.
Obtains 16.0.
Multiplies q₁ by ratio from (b) with positive sign.
Obtains q₂ = +3.20 × 10⁻⁸ C.

items.stem: Two opposite point charges, +4 nC (left) and −4 nC (right), are fixed 0.4 m apart. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.2 m from +4 nC, where the electric potential is zero. Assume a vacuum with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero potential at infinity. What is the resultant electric field at point P?
items.workedSolution: Even though V = kq₁/r₁ + kq₂/r₂ = 0 at P, the potential gradient dV/dx is non-zero because both opposite charges drive a positive test charge to the right: E = 899 N C⁻¹ + 899 N C⁻¹ = 1.80 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (A).

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes E != 0 when V = 0 and adds the field contributions along the line to obtain 1.80 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (A).

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates are separated by 0.08 m in a vacuum, with a potential difference of 1600 V between them. A small charged sphere of charge +1.5 × 10⁻⁸ C and mass 3 × 10⁻⁶ kg moves from the positive plate to the earthed 0 V plate. Calculate the work done by the uniform electric field as the sphere moves to the 0 V plate.
items.workedSolution: Electrical work done across the full potential difference is W = qΔV = (1.5 × 10⁻⁸)(1600) = 2.40 × 10⁻⁵ J (D).

items.stem: In a uniform electric field, three equally spaced parallel equipotential lines are 0.02 m apart. Their potentials from left to right are 180 V, 100 V, and 20 V. A Millikan oil droplet of charge +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ C and mass 3.2 × 10⁻¹³ kg is released from rest on the 100 V line and moves horizontally without friction. Calculate the speed of the Millikan oil droplet when it reaches the 20 V line.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ½mv² = q(V₁ − V₂) with ΔV = 80 V to obtain 0.894 m s⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: What physical process produces the characteristic coloured glow observed inside the positive column of a low-pressure gas-discharge tube?
items.workedSolution: Inside the discharge tube, electrons collide with and excite gas atoms which emit visible photons on de-excitation, giving each gas its signature colour.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that electrons collide with and excite gas atoms which emit visible photons on de-excitation.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that uniform parallel magnetic field lines inside the air-core solenoid resembling a bar magnet outside.

options.text: The magnetic field is strictly zero inside the air core and uniform everywhere outside the windings.
options.distractorRationale: The field is strongest and uniform inside the solenoid core, not zero.

options.label: B
options.text: It consists of uniform parallel magnetic field lines inside the air-core solenoid resembling a bar magnet outside, with closed loops returning from one end to the other.

options.label: C
options.text: Field lines form isolated concentric circles strictly perpendicular to the solenoid axis with zero axial field.
options.distractorRationale: Superposition of adjacent turns cancels radial components inside and reinforces a strong axial field.

options.label: D
options.text: Field lines start on one end of the solenoid and terminate permanently at infinity without closing.
options.distractorRationale: Magnetic field lines always form continuous closed loops.

items.stem: Two point charges, +4 nC on the left and −12 nC on the right, are fixed 0.8 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.5 m from the +4 nC charge. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electric potential at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) Scalar potential V = k(q₁/0.5 + q₂/0.3) = −288 V. (b) Vector electric field E = 1.34 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: A slab of polar dielectric material is slid smoothly to fill the air gap between the charged plates of a parallel-plate capacitor. How do the polar molecules increase the capacitance?
items.workedSolution: In the applied field, polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity. Therefore the correct statement is: The polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity

options.label: A
options.text: The polar molecules conduct free electrons directly across the gap to equalise plate potentials.
options.distractorRationale: A dielectric is an insulator; conduction across the gap would discharge the capacitor.

options.label: B
options.text: The polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity

options.label: C
options.text: The polar molecules align positive ends toward the positive plate, reinforcing the applied field and raising potential difference.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses dipole orientation and electric field direction.

options.label: D
options.text: The polar molecules physically push the metal plates further apart so capacitance increases with separation.
options.distractorRationale: Increasing separation d decreases capacitance since C = ε₀εᵣA/d.

items.stem: Two point charges, −8 nC (left) and +5 nC (right), are held 0.7 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line joining them, 0.3 m to the right of the −8 nC charge. Use the Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Calculate the magnitude and direction of the resultant electric field at point P.
items.workedSolution: At P, both opposite-sign sources drive a positive test charge to the left. |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 799 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 281 N C⁻¹ (with r₂ = 0.4 m). Summing the two same-sense vectors gives E = 1.08 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (D).

markScheme.criterion: Adds same-direction inverse-square contributions to obtain 1.08 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (D).

items.stem: Consider the V–r graph outside a planet and the V–r graph outside a positively charged isolated sphere. Why do the two curves lie on opposite sides of the horizontal V = 0 axis?
items.workedSolution: At infinity V = 0: gravity is always attractive (V < 0), while a positive source repels a positive test charge (V > 0). Therefore the correct statement is: Using the zero-at-infinity convention, gravitational potential is always negative and rises toward zero at infinity because gravity is attractive, whereas electric potential around a positive charge is positive and falls toward zero at infinity.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: gravitational potential is always negative and rises toward zero at infinity because gravity is attractive, whereas electric potential around a positive charge is positive and falls toward zero at infinity.

options.label: A
options.text: Gravitational potential is positive near a planet because work is released as a mass is lifted away to infinity.
options.distractorRationale: External work must be done ON a mass to lift it against attractive gravity to infinity (V = 0), so V must be negative everywhere finite.

options.label: B
options.text: Using the zero-at-infinity convention, gravitational potential is always negative and rises toward zero at infinity because gravity is attractive, whereas electric potential around a positive charge is positive and falls toward zero at infinity.

options.label: C
options.text: Electric potential around a positive charge is negative because a positive test charge is attracted inward toward the source.
options.distractorRationale: Like positive charges repel, so work is done pushing a positive test charge inward from infinity, making V positive.

options.label: D
options.text: Both potentials are actually positive, but gravitational potential is plotted downward solely to prevent the curves overlapping.
options.distractorRationale: The negative sign of V = −GM/r is physically essential, not an arbitrary plotting choice.

items.stem: Three parallel equipotential lines lie in a uniform electric field, spaced 0.06 m apart. From left to right, their potentials are 120 V, 0 V, and -120 V. A particle of charge +5 × 10⁻⁹ C moves from the 120 V line to the -120 V line. Calculate the signed change in electric potential energy ΔE_p of the charge.
items.workedSolution: Change in electric potential energy is ΔE_p = q(V_final − V_initial) = (+5 × 10⁻⁹ C)(-120 − (120)) = −1.20 × 10⁻⁶ J (D).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p = q(V_f − V_i) = −1.20 × 10⁻⁶ J (D).

items.stem: An alpha particle of charge +2e approaches a stationary gold nucleus of charge +79e head-on. Their minimum centre-to-centre separation is 3.8 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and zero electric potential at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) V = kZe / r_min = 2.99 × 10⁶ V. (b) E_p = 2eV = 9.57 × 10⁻¹³ J. (c) Dividing by e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ gives 5.98 × 10⁶ eV.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes Q = 79e and r_min = 3.8 × 10⁻¹⁴ m into V = kQ/r.
Obtains 2.99 × 10⁶ V.
Multiplies potential from (a) by projectile charge 2e.
Obtains 9.57 × 10⁻¹³ J.
Divides joule energy by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ (or multiplies V in volts by z).
Obtains 5.98 × 10⁶ eV.

Calculate the electrostatic potential energy (in joules) of the alpha particle at closest approach.
Express this electrostatic potential energy in electronvolts (eV).
workingSteps: E_p (in eV) = E_p (in J) / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹) = 5.98 × 10⁶ eV.

items.stem: Two positive point charges, +32 nC on the left and +2 nC on the right, are fixed 0.85 m apart in a vacuum. Assume a vacuum with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero potential at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) Setting 32/x² = 2/(0.85 − x)² gives x = 0.680 m. (b) Scalar potentials add: V = k(q₁/x + q₂/(d − x)) = 529 V. (c) By definition of the null point (zero potential gradient), E = 0 N C⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Equates 32/x² = 2/(0.85 − x)².
Obtains x = 0.680 m.
Adds positive scalar potential contributions kq₁/x + kq₂/(d − x).
Obtains V = 529 V.
States 0 N C⁻¹.

items.stem: A charged oil droplet of weight $2.84 \times 10^{-14}\text{ N}$ is held motionless between parallel plates 10.0 mm apart by a potential difference of 592 V. Given $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, how many excess elementary charges are on the droplet?
items.workedSolution: $Q = \frac{Wd}{V} = \frac{2.84 \times 10^{-14} \times 0.0100}{592} = 4.80 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$. Dividing by $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$ gives $n = 3.0$ excess electrons.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 3.0.

items.stem: High-voltage electrostatic generators use large, smoothly polished spherical domes rather than small or sharp-pointed terminals.
items.workedSolution: Excess charge resides entirely on the outer conducting surface so the electric field inside is zero and the entire sphere is an equipotential. Inside the conductor E = 0 and excess charge spreads uniformly across the smooth outer surface. Outside, surface field strength is E_surf = Q/(4πε₀R²) = V/R. Air ionises and sparks once E_surf reaches the dielectric breakdown field E_max (~3 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹). Therefore maximum potential V_max = E_max R scales linearly with R, capacitance C = 4πε₀R scales with R, and maximum stored energy E = ½CV_max² = 2πε₀ E_max² R³ scales as R³. Smooth curvature avoids sharp points where local field concentration triggers premature corona discharge.

markScheme.criterion: L1: States excess charge resides on the outer surface with zero electric field inside the conducting dome.
L1: Links surface field strength to potential and radius via E = V/R = Q/(4πε₀R²).
L2: Explains air breaks down (ionises and sparks) when surface field reaches a fixed threshold E_max.
L2: Deduces maximum achievable potential V_max = E_max R increases linearly with sphere radius R.
L3: Combines C = 4πε₀R with E = ½CV² to show maximum stored energy scales rapidly as R³.
L3: Explains sharp points have tiny local radius of curvature creating intense local electric fields and premature corona discharge.

parts.prompt: Explain why a large, smooth conducting sphere can reach a much higher potential and store far more electrostatic energy before air breaks down into a spark, referencing interior field, surface field E = V/R, and C = 4πε₀R. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Excess charge resides entirely on the outer conducting surface so the electric field inside is zero and the entire sphere is an equipotential. Inside the conductor E = 0 and excess charge spreads uniformly across the smooth outer surface. Outside, surface field strength is E_surf = Q/(4πε₀R²) = V/R. Air ionises and sparks once E_surf reaches the dielectric breakdown field E_max (~3 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹). Therefore maximum potential V_max = E_max R scales linearly with R, capacitance C = 4πε₀R scales with R, and maximum stored energy E = ½CV_max² = 2πε₀ E_max² R³ scales as R³. Smooth curvature avoids sharp points where local field concentration triggers premature corona discharge.
workingSteps: Describe uniform surface charge distribution and E = 0 inside a smooth conducting sphere.
Relate surface field E = V/R to dielectric breakdown limit of air, giving V_max = E_max R.
Combine with C = 4πε₀R to show E_max_stored ∝ R³ and explain why sharp points cause corona leakage.

items.stem: Two point charges, +9Q on the left and +2Q on the right, are fixed a distance 3 x apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 2 x from the left charge. Using the Coulomb constant k, express the resultant electric field at P in terms of kQ/x².
items.workedSolution: At P, +9Q produces (9/2²) kQ/x² = 2.25 kQ/x² to the right, while +2Q at distance 1 x produces (2/1²) kQ/x² = 2.00 kQ/x² to the left. Net field = 0.250 kQ/x² to the right (C).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts (9/2²) and (2/1²) to obtain 0.250 kQ/x² to the right (C).

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates in a vacuum are 0.06 m apart and held at 1200 V and 0 V. An alpha particle of mass 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and charge +3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is released from rest at the 1200 V plate. Neglecting gravity, calculate the speed of the alpha particle when it reaches the 0 V plate.
items.workedSolution: By conservation of energy, ½mv² = qV, so v = √(2qV / m) = √(2 × 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1200 / 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷) = 3.40 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (C).

markScheme.criterion: Equates ½mv² = qV to obtain v = 3.40 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: Two point charges, +8 nC (left) and +2 nC (right), are held 0.5 m apart along a straight line. Point P lies between them, 0.2 m from the +8 nC charge. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Both positive sources repel a positive test charge placed at P, so the left charge pushes rightward while the right charge pushes leftward. (b) |E₁| = k|q₁|/(0.2)² = 1.80 × 10³ N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/(0.3)² = 200 N C⁻¹. Subtracting the opposing vectors yields 1.60 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: States that a positive test charge between like-sign sources experiences opposite forces from the left and right charges.
Evaluates E = k|q|/r² at r₁ = 0.2 m and r₂ = 0.3 m.
Subtracts the two opposing field magnitudes.
Obtains 1.60 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: Point charges −7 nC at x = 0 and +7 nC at x = 0.7 m are fixed in a vacuum. At point P on the axis (x = 0.35 m), the electric potential is zero. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², with V = 0 at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) V = k(-7 × 10⁻⁹/0.35 + 7 × 10⁻⁹/0.35) = 0 V. (b) At P both fields point to the left, giving E = 514 N C⁻¹ + 514 N C⁻¹ = 1.03 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes signed charges with r₁ = 0.35 m and r₂ = 0.35 m into V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂).
Obtains V = 0 V.
Applies inverse-square law E = k|q|/r² to both sources.
Adds the two electric field magnitudes.
Obtains 1.03 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates are 0.04 m apart with a potential difference of 2000 V (from 2000 V on the left plate to 0 V on the right plate). Obtains 5.00 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.
Applies W = qV (or W = qEd).
Obtains 1.60 × 10⁻⁵ J.

items.stem: In a uniform electric field, three equally spaced parallel equipotential lines are 0.055 m apart. Their potentials from left to right are 260 V, 150 V, and 40 V. items.workedSolution: (a) E = (150 − 40) / 0.055 = 2.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right. (b) a = qE / m = 3.64 m s⁻². (c) Using ½mv² = q(110), v = 0.632 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Divides adjacent potential step by spacing s.
Obtains 2.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right.
Applies a = qE / m.
Obtains 3.64 m s⁻².
Equates ½mv² = q(110) or uses v² = 2as.
Obtains 0.632 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: An electron has rest energy $0.511\text{ MeV}$ and travels at $v = 0.920c$. Calculate its relativistic kinetic energy $E_{\text{k}} = E - m_0 c^2$ in MeV.
items.workedSolution: $\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.920^2}} = 2.55$. Kinetic energy $E_{\text{k}} = (\gamma - 1)(0.511\text{ MeV}) = 0.793 MeV$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 0.793 MeV.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Reports total energy $\gamma m_0 c^2$ without subtracting rest energy $m_0 c^2$.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the classical expression $\frac{1}{2}m_0 v^2$ instead of relativistic $(\gamma - 1)m_0 c^2$.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes relativistic mass into the classical $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ formula.

items.stem: Two small charged spheres carrying $+4.0\text{ }\mu\text{C}$ and $+6.0\text{ }\mu\text{C}$ are separated by $10.0\text{ cm}$ inside insulating oil of permittivity $\varepsilon = 2.50\,\varepsilon_0$. What is the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them?
items.workedSolution: Using $F = \frac{q_1 q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon r^2}$ with $\varepsilon = 2.50 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^2\text{ N}^{-1}\text{ m}^{-2}$ and $r = 0.100\text{ m}$ gives $F = 8.63 N$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 8.63 N.

items.workedSolution: Electric potential is a signed scalar: V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂) with r₁ = 0.2 m and r₂ = 0.4 m. Thus V = −180 V + (−180 V) = −360 V (D).

markScheme.criterion: Sums signed scalar potentials kq₁/0.2 + kq₂/0.4 = −360 V (D).

items.stem: An air-filled parallel-plate capacitor is charged to voltage V and then disconnected from the battery so it is electrically isolated. A polar dielectric slab of relative permittivity εᵣ is then inserted between the plates. What happens to its voltage and stored energy?
items.workedSolution: For an isolated capacitor, charge stays constant so potential difference and stored energy decrease by factor relative permittivity. Therefore the correct statement is: Because it is isolated, charge stays constant so potential difference and stored energy decrease by factor relative permittivity

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: charge stays constant so potential difference and stored energy decrease by factor relative permittivity.

items.stem: Two point charges, +2.5 nC (left) and −5 nC (right), are held 0.5 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line joining them, 0.2 m to the right of the +2.5 nC charge. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Both individual electric field vectors at P point to the right (away from the positive left source and toward the negative right source), so they reinforce toward the right. (b) With r₁ = 0.2 m and r₂ = 0.3 m, |E₁| = 562 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = 499 N C⁻¹. Summing gives 1.06 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

parts.prompt: State and explain why the two individual electric field contributions reinforce rather than oppose each other at point P.
parts.expectedAnswer: Both individual electric field vectors at P point to the right (away from the positive left source and toward the negative right source), so they reinforce toward the right.
workingSteps: Electric field direction is the force direction on a positive test charge.
Both individual electric field vectors at P point to the right (away from the positive left source and toward the negative right source), so they reinforce toward the right.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude and state the direction of the resultant electric field at point P.
workingSteps: |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 562 N C⁻¹; |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 499 N C⁻¹.
Resultant E = |E₁| + |E₂| = 1.06 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: Fixed point charges +11 nC (left) and −4 nC (right) are separated by 0.7 m in free space. A probe charge of −2.2 nC is held at point P, 0.3 m from the +11 nC charge. Use 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², with zero electric potential at infinity. Calculate the electric potential at P due to the two fixed source charges.
items.workedSolution: Electric potential at P depends only on the source charges: V = k(q₁/0.3 + q₂/0.4) = 330 V + (−89.9 V) = 240 V (D).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = k(q₁/0.3 + q₂/0.4) = 240 V (D), independent of q_test.

items.stem: Two point charges, −12 nC on the left and +5 nC on the right, are fixed 0.4 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line to the right of both charges, 0.7 m from the −12 nC charge. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Calculate the magnitude and direction of the resultant electric field at point P.
items.workedSolution: Exterior point P is r₁ = 0.7 m to the right of −12 nC and r₂ = 0.7 − 0.4 = 0.3 m to the right of +5 nC. Superposing E_x = kq₁/r₁² + kq₂/r₂² gives 279 N C⁻¹ to the right (D).

markScheme.criterion: Uses r₁ = 0.7 m and r₂ = 0.3 m to obtain 279 N C⁻¹ to the right (D).

items.stem: Two point charges are fixed on the x-axis in a vacuum: +4 nC at x = 0 and +16 nC at x = 0.9 m. At what distance from the +4 nC charge between them is the resultant electric field zero?
items.workedSolution: Equating opposing field magnitudes gives q₁/x² = q₂/(0.9 − x)², so (0.9 − x)/x = √(16/4). Solving yields x = 0.9 × √4/(√4 + √16) = 0.300 m (B).

markScheme.criterion: Equates kq₁/x² = kq₂/(0.9 − x)² to obtain x = 0.300 m (B).

items.stem: Two stationary point charges, +6 nC (left) and −3 nC (right), are held 0.5 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.2 m from the left charge. A small test charge of −4 nC is placed at P without moving the fixed charges. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Calculate the resultant electric force on the −4 nC test charge.
items.workedSolution: At P (r₁ = 0.2 m, r₂ = 0.3 m), the resultant electric field is E = 1.65 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right. Multiplying by q_test = −4 nC gives F = q_test E = 6.59 × 10⁻⁶ N to the left (A).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates E = 1.65 × 10³ N C⁻¹ and F = qE = 6.59 × 10⁻⁶ N to the left (A).

items.stem: An alpha particle of charge +2e approaches a stationary bismuth nucleus head-on. The nucleus has atomic number Z = 83 (charge +83e), and the distance of closest approach is r_min = 5.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and zero electric potential at infinity. What is the electric potential due to the bismuth nucleus at distance r_min?
items.workedSolution: Radial potential of the +83e nucleus is V = kZe / r_min = (8.99 × 10⁹ × 83 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) / (5.2 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 2.30 × 10⁶ V (A).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = kZe / r_min = 2.30 × 10⁶ V (A).

items.stem: Two fixed point charges of +1 nC (left) and +25 nC (right) are separated by 0.6 m in free space. Use 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², with zero electric potential at infinity. Calculate the electric potential at the point between the charges where the resultant electric field is zero.
items.workedSolution: Zero field occurs at x = 0.6 × √1/(√1 + √25) = 0.100 m from +1 nC (and 0.500 m from +25 nC). Scalar potentials add: V = k(q₁/x + q₂/(d − x)) = 539 V (C).

markScheme.criterion: Finds x = 0.100 m and sums positive scalar potentials to obtain 539 V (C).

items.stem: An isolated hollow metal dome of radius $R$ stands on an insulating column in air. How is its capacitance formula derived from electrostatics?
items.workedSolution: From V = Q/(4πε₀R) and C = Q/V, dividing Q by V yields C = 4πε₀R directly proportional to sphere radius R. Therefore the correct statement is: Combining C = Q over V with radial surface potential V = Q over 4 pi epsilon zero R gives isolated sphere capacitance C = 4 pi epsilon zero R.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: combining C = Q over V with radial surface potential V = Q over 4 pi epsilon zero R gives isolated sphere capacitance C = 4 pi epsilon zero R.

options.label: A
options.text: Equating surface field E = Q/(4πε₀R²) to Q/V gives C = 4πε₀R², proportional to surface area.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses electric field strength E with electric potential V; capacitance depends on V = Q/(4πε₀R), not E.

options.label: B
options.text: Combining C = Q over V with radial surface potential V = Q over 4 pi epsilon zero R gives isolated sphere capacitance C = 4 pi epsilon zero R.

options.label: C
options.text: Using the parallel-plate formula with area 4πR² and separation R gives C = 4πε₀/R, inversely proportional to radius.
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the dependence on R; a larger sphere stores more charge per volt so C increases linearly with R.

options.label: D
options.text: Because there is no second nearby plate, an isolated conducting sphere has strictly zero capacitance.
options.distractorRationale: An isolated sphere stores charge relative to zero potential at infinity, giving finite capacitance C = 4πε₀R.

items.stem: Two positive point charges, +10Q and +4Q, are fixed a distance 3 x apart in a vacuum, with +10Q on the left. Point P lies between them at a distance 2 x from +10Q. Write the magnitude of the resultant electric field at P in the form E = α kQ/x², where k is the Coulomb constant.
items.workedSolution: (a) The right positive charge produces a larger repulsive field magnitude at P than the left positive charge, so the net electric field points to the left. (b) α = |10/2² − 4/1²| = |2.50 − 4.00| = 1.50.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies resultant direction as to the left with valid reasoning.
Forms inverse-square terms 10/2² and 4/1².
Subtracts the opposing dimensionless field coefficients.
Obtains α = 1.50.

items.stem: Two point charges are fixed 0.8 m apart in a vacuum: q₁ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ C on the left and q₂ on the right. The net electric field is zero at a point between them, 0.5 m from q₁.
items.workedSolution: (a) q₁ and q₂ have the same sign so their fields oppose between them. (b) |q₂/q₁| = ((0.8 − 0.5)/0.5)² = (0.3/0.5)² = 0.360. (c) q₂ = +(0.360)(2.5 × 10⁻⁸ C) = +9.00 × 10⁻⁹ C.

markScheme.criterion: States same sign because fields must oppose in the region between the charges.
Uses |q₂/q₁| = ((d − x₀)/x₀)² with d − x₀ = 0.3 m.
Obtains 0.360.
Multiplies q₁ by ratio from (b) with positive sign.
Obtains q₂ = +9.00 × 10⁻⁹ C.

items.stem: Two point charges, +5 nC (left) and +12 nC (right), are held 0.8 m apart along a straight line. Point P lies between them, 0.5 m from the +5 nC charge. Use the Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the resultant electric field at point P?
items.workedSolution: Between like-sign charges, the individual fields at P oppose each other: |E₁| = k|q₁|/(0.5)² = 180 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/(0.3)² = 1.20 × 10³ N C⁻¹. Subtracting gives |E_net| = 1.02 × 10³ N C⁻¹ directed to the left (C).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts opposing inverse-square field contributions to obtain 1.02 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (C).

items.stem: Two point charges, +6 nC on the left and −12 nC on the right, are fixed 0.9 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.3 m from the left charge. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and V = 0 at infinity. Although the electric potential at P is zero, determine the resultant electric field at P.
items.workedSolution: Even though V = kq₁/r₁ + kq₂/r₂ = 0 at P, the potential gradient dV/dx is non-zero because both opposite charges drive a positive test charge to the right: E = 599 N C⁻¹ + 300 N C⁻¹ = 899 N C⁻¹ to the right (D).

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes E != 0 when V = 0 and adds the field contributions along the line to obtain 899 N C⁻¹ to the right (D).

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates are 0.032 m apart in a vacuum with a potential difference of 640 V. A small charged particle of mass 7 × 10⁻⁶ kg and charge +3.5 × 10⁻⁸ C moves from the +640 V plate to the 0 V plate. Neglecting edge effects, calculate the uniform electric field strength between the plates.
items.workedSolution: For uniform parallel plates, E = V / d = 640 / 0.032 = 2.00 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: In a uniform electric field, three equally spaced parallel equipotential lines are 0.03 m apart. Their potentials from left to right are 280 V, 160 V, and 40 V. A charged bead of mass 2.7 × 10⁻⁵ kg and charge +4.5 × 10⁻⁸ C starts from rest on the middle 160 V line. It moves horizontally without friction to the 40 V line. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the uniform electric field.
items.workedSolution: Electric field points toward decreasing potential (to the right) with magnitude E = |ΔV|/s = (160 − 40) / 0.03 = 4.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right (B).

markScheme.criterion: Uses E = −ΔV/Δx to obtain 4.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right (B).

items.stem: Looking at the graph of relativistic mass $m / m_0$ against speed $v / c$, what physical consequence follows from the vertical asymptote at $v = c$?
items.workedSolution: As $v \to c$, $\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} \to 0$ so relativistic mass approaches infinity as speed approaches c requiring infinite energy.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that relativistic mass approaches infinity as speed approaches c requiring infinite energy.

options.label: A
options.text: Because relativistic mass approaches infinity as speed approaches c requiring infinite energy, no particle with non-zero rest mass can ever be accelerated to or beyond the speed of light $c$.

options.label: B
options.text: A particle's mass drops smoothly to zero at v = c so it glides past c effortlessly.
options.distractorRationale: Mass increases without bound as $v \to c$, rather than dropping to zero.

options.label: C
options.text: Relativistic mass grows linearly with speed so doubling kinetic energy always doubles speed.
options.distractorRationale: The curve bends sharply upward toward infinity at $v = c$, deviating drastically from classical mechanics.

options.label: D
options.text: Particles exceed c once their mass reaches 5 m₀ in a particle accelerator.
options.distractorRationale: Even when $m \gg 5 m_0$, speed always remains less than $c$.

items.stem: The diagram shows the cross-section of a long straight conductor carrying conventional current directly out of the page (indicated by $\odot$). Which description correctly identifies the magnetic field lines in the plane of the page?
items.workedSolution: Pointing the right-hand thumb out of the page along the conventional current curls the fingers anticlockwise, giving anticlockwise circular magnetic field lines centred on the wire around the wire.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that anticlockwise circular magnetic field lines centred on the wire around the wire.

items.stem: Two point charges, −10 nC on the left and +4 nC on the right, are fixed 0.7 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.3 m from the −10 nC charge. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electric potential at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) Scalar potential V = k(q₁/0.3 + q₂/0.4) = −210 V. (b) Vector electric field E = 1.22 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

markScheme.criterion: Applies signed scalar sum V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂).
Obtains V = −210 V (including sign if negative).
Uses inverse-square magnitudes at r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.4 m.
Combines the two electric field vectors along the line with proper directions.
Obtains 1.22 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

items.stem: An air-spaced parallel-plate capacitor is charged to 27.0 V and isolated from the power supply. A polar dielectric slab of relative permittivity 3.60 is then inserted to fill the gap. Calculate the new potential difference across the plates.
items.workedSolution: Isolated Q is fixed and C' = εᵣC, so V' = Q / C' = V₀ / εᵣ = 27.0 / 3.60 = 7.50 V.

markScheme.criterion: Computes V' = V₀ / εᵣ = 7.50 V.

items.stem: Two fixed point charges, +2 nC on the left and −9 nC on the right, are 0.5 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.2 m from the +2 nC charge. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Determine the magnitude and direction of the net electric field at point P.
items.workedSolution: At P, both opposite-sign sources drive a positive test charge to the right. |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 449 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 899 N C⁻¹ (with r₂ = 0.3 m). Summing the two same-sense vectors gives E = 1.35 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (D).

markScheme.criterion: Adds same-direction inverse-square contributions to obtain 1.35 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (D).

items.stem: Two point charges, +6 nC on the left and +9 nC on the right, are fixed 0.6 m apart in a vacuum. A small test charge of −1.5 nC is placed at point P, 0.2 m from +6 nC. Take 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electric potential at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) E = 843 N C⁻¹ to the right. (b) Scalar sum V = k(q₁/0.2 + q₂/0.4) = 472 V. (c) Force on probe F = q_test E = 1.26 × 10⁻⁶ N to the left.

Obtains 843 N C⁻¹ to the right.

Obtains 472 V.
Uses F = q_test E with correct sign/direction.
Obtains 1.26 × 10⁻⁶ N to the left.

items.stem: Two point charges, +12 nC (left) and −3 nC (right), are fixed 0.3 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line beyond the right-hand charge, 0.5 m from +12 nC. Use the Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Because P lies to the right of both opposite-sign charges, one source repels a positive test charge rightward while the other attracts it leftward, so their fields oppose. (b) Using r₁ = 0.5 m and r₂ = 0.2 m, |E₁| = 432 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = 674 N C⁻¹, giving resultant E = 243 N C⁻¹ to the left.

Obtains 243 N C⁻¹ to the left.

parts.expectedAnswer: Because P lies to the right of both opposite-sign charges, one source repels a positive test charge rightward while the other attracts it leftward, so their fields oppose.
workingSteps: Because P lies to the right of both opposite-sign charges, one source repels a positive test charge rightward while the other attracts it leftward, so their fields oppose.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude and state the direction of the resultant electric field at exterior point P.
workingSteps: Distances to P: r₁ = 0.5 m and r₂ = 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.2 m.
Resultant E = 243 N C⁻¹ to the left.

items.stem: Two point charges are fixed on the x-axis in a vacuum: +4 nC at x = 0 and +25 nC at x = 0.7 m.
items.workedSolution: (a) Between two positive charges their repulsive fields act in opposite directions, and equal field magnitudes require a smaller distance from the weaker left-hand charge. (b) Setting 4/x² = 25/(0.7 − x)² gives (0.7 − x)/x = √(25/4), hence x = 0.200 m.

markScheme.criterion: Explains opposing fields between positive sources and identifies closer proximity to the left-hand charge.
Equates inverse-square field magnitudes 4/x² = 25/(0.7 − x)².
Takes square roots correctly to linearize for x.
Obtains x = 0.200 m.

items.stem: Two fixed point charges of +12 nC (left) and −6 nC (right) are 0.8 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line joining them, 0.3 m from the left charge. Use the Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) With r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.5 m, superposing the two inverse-square fields gives E = 1.41 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right. (b) Using F = q_test E with q_test = +1.5 nC gives F = 2.12 × 10⁻⁶ N to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Uses E = k|q|/r² with r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.5 m.
Combines the two electric field vectors along the line with correct signs.
Obtains 1.41 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.
Multiplies field from (a) by probe charge in coulombs.
Obtains 2.12 × 10⁻⁶ N to the right.

items.stem: In a uniform electric field, three parallel equipotential surfaces are separated by 0.04 m. Their potentials from left to right are -150 V, -50 V, and 50 V. A particle of charge −2 × 10⁻⁸ C moves from the -150 V line to the 50 V line. Calculate the signed work done by the electric field on the charge.
items.workedSolution: Work done by the electric field is W_field = q(V_initial − V_final) = (−2 × 10⁻⁸ C)(-150 − (50)) = 4.00 × 10⁻⁶ J (A).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates W_field = q(V_i − V_f) = 4.00 × 10⁻⁶ J (A).

items.stem: A stationary lead nucleus of charge +82e repels a triply charged lithium nucleus of charge +3e approaching head-on. The incoming particle comes to rest at a separation of 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and zero electric potential at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) V = kZe / r_min = 1.84 × 10⁶ V. (b) E_p = 3eV = 8.85 × 10⁻¹³ J. (c) Dividing by e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ gives 5.53 × 10⁶ eV.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes Q = 82e and r_min = 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ m into V = kQ/r.
Obtains 1.84 × 10⁶ V.
Multiplies potential from (a) by projectile charge 3e.
Obtains 8.85 × 10⁻¹³ J.
Divides joule energy by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ (or multiplies V in volts by z).

parts.prompt: Calculate the electric potential due to the lead nucleus at distance r_min.
Calculate the electrostatic potential energy (in joules) of the triply charged lithium nucleus at closest approach.
Express this electrostatic potential energy in electronvolts (eV).
workingSteps: E_p (in eV) = E_p (in J) / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹) = 5.53 × 10⁶ eV.

items.stem: Two fixed point charges of +8 nC (left) and +2 nC (right) are separated by 0.75 m in free space. Use 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², with zero electric potential at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) Setting 8/x² = 2/(0.75 − x)² gives x = 0.500 m. (b) Scalar potentials add: V = k(q₁/x + q₂/(d − x)) = 216 V. (c) By definition of the null point (zero potential gradient), E = 0 N C⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Equates 8/x² = 2/(0.75 − x)².
Obtains x = 0.500 m.
Adds positive scalar potential contributions kq₁/x + kq₂/(d − x).
Obtains V = 216 V.
States 0 N C⁻¹.

items.stem: When deriving the radius of a falling Millikan droplet from $6\pi\eta r v = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho g$, which physical assumptions are required?
items.workedSolution: Applying $6\pi\eta r v = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho g$ requires that the droplet is spherical moves slowly in laminar airflow and upthrust from air is negligible.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that droplet is spherical moves slowly in laminar airflow and upthrust from air is negligible.

options.text: The droplet is cubical moves at turbulent high speed and experiences zero viscous drag.
options.distractorRationale: Stokes' law applies only to slow laminar flow around a sphere.
