options.label: C
options.text: The chamber is fully evacuated so air viscosity drops to zero during terminal fall.
options.distractorRationale: Air viscosity is essential to establish a measurable terminal speed when the electric field is off.

options.label: D
options.text: Air density exceeds oil density so upward buoyancy dominates over weight.
options.distractorRationale: Oil density is ~700 times air density, making air upthrust negligible.

items.stem: Isolated sphere 1 (radius 24.0 cm) is charged to 40.0 kV, then joined by closing switch S to an initially uncharged sphere 2 (radius 16.0 cm). Taking $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F m}^{-1}$ and $C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 R$, calculate the total electrostatic energy dissipated in the wire and spark in millijoules.
items.workedSolution: E_i = ½C₁V₁² = 21.4 mJ; V_f = 40.0 × 24/40 = 24.0 kV, so E_f = ½(C₁ + C₂)V_f² = 12.8 mJ. Energy dissipated ΔE = 21.4 − 12.8 = 8.54 mJ.

markScheme.criterion: Computes ΔE = E_i − E_f = 8.54 mJ.

items.stem: Two positive point charges, +4Q on the left and +18Q on the right, are fixed a distance 4 x apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 1 x from +4Q and 3 x from +18Q. Using the Coulomb constant k, express the resultant electric field at P in terms of kQ/x².
items.workedSolution: At P, +4Q produces (4/1²) kQ/x² = 4.00 kQ/x² to the right, while +18Q at distance 3 x produces (18/3²) kQ/x² = 2.00 kQ/x² to the left. Net field = 2.00 kQ/x² to the right (D).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts (4/1²) and (18/3²) to obtain 2.00 kQ/x² to the right (D).

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates in a vacuum are 0.04 m apart and held at 600 V and 0 V. A charged polymer droplet of mass 1.2 × 10⁻⁹ kg and charge +4 × 10⁻¹² C is released from rest at the 600 V plate. Neglecting gravity, calculate the speed of the charged polymer droplet when it reaches the 0 V plate.
items.workedSolution: By conservation of energy, ½mv² = qV, so v = √(2qV / m) = √(2 × 4 × 10⁻¹² × 600 / 1.2 × 10⁻⁹) = 2.00 m s⁻¹ (B).

markScheme.criterion: Equates ½mv² = qV to obtain v = 2.00 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: Two point charges, +9 nC on the left and +3 nC on the right, are fixed 0.6 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies between them, 0.2 m from the left charge. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the resultant electric field at point P?
items.workedSolution: Between like-sign charges, the individual fields at P oppose each other: |E₁| = k|q₁|/(0.2)² = 2.02 × 10³ N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/(0.4)² = 169 N C⁻¹. Subtracting gives |E_net| = 1.85 × 10³ N C⁻¹ directed to the right (A).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts opposing inverse-square field contributions to obtain 1.85 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (A).

items.stem: Two opposite point charges of −2 nC (left) and +6 nC (right) are 0.8 m apart in free space. Point P is between them, 0.2 m from the left-hand charge. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², with zero potential at infinity. Although the electric potential at P is zero, what is the resultant electric field at P?
items.workedSolution: Even though V = kq₁/r₁ + kq₂/r₂ = 0 at P, the potential gradient dV/dx is non-zero because both opposite charges drive a positive test charge to the left: E = 449 N C⁻¹ + 150 N C⁻¹ = 599 N C⁻¹ to the left (D).

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes E != 0 when V = 0 and adds the field contributions along the line to obtain 599 N C⁻¹ to the left (D).

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates are 0.06 m apart in a vacuum and are held at 1200 V and 0 V. A charged bead of mass 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ kg and charge +1.25 × 10⁻⁸ C accelerates across the gap. Calculate the uniform electric field strength between the plates.
items.workedSolution: For uniform parallel plates, E = V / d = 1200 / 0.06 = 2.00 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: An electron in a linear accelerator reaches speed $v = 0.800c$. Using the relativistic mass relation $m = \frac{m_0}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}$, calculate the relativistic mass ratio $m / m_0$ plotted on the vertical axis.
items.workedSolution: Relativistic mass ratio $\frac{m}{m_0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.800^2}} = \frac{1}{0.600} = 1.67$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 1.67.

items.stem: An isolated hollow conducting sphere of radius $R = 8.0\text{ cm}$ carries a total charge of $+24.0\text{ nC}$ distributed over its outer surface. Taking zero potential at infinity, what is the electric potential at a point $3.0\text{ cm}$ from the centre inside the hollow cavity?
items.workedSolution: Inside a charged conducting sphere $E = 0$, so the potential is uniform everywhere inside and equals the surface potential: $V_{\text{e}} = \frac{kQ}{R} = \frac{8.99 \times 10^9 \times 24.0 \times 10^{-9}}{0.080} = 2.70 × 10³ V$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 2.70 × 10³ V.

items.stem: Two point charges, +15 nC on the left and −6 nC on the right, are fixed 0.9 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.5 m from the +15 nC charge. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electric potential at infinity. Determine the electric potential at point P.
items.workedSolution: Electric potential is a signed scalar: V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂) with r₁ = 0.5 m and r₂ = 0.4 m. Thus V = 270 V + (−135 V) = 135 V (C).

markScheme.criterion: Sums signed scalar potentials kq₁/0.5 + kq₂/0.4 = 135 V (C).

items.stem: In an RC circuit, a student replaces the charging resistor with one of four times the resistance. The student then recharges the same empty capacitor using the same ideal battery. How does the total thermal energy dissipated in the resistor change?
items.workedSolution: Regardless of R, the battery supplies energy Q V while the capacitor stores half Q V so exactly fifty percent is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of resistance value. Therefore the correct statement is: It is unchanged because the battery supplies energy Q V while the capacitor stores half Q V so exactly fifty percent is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of resistance value

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: battery supplies energy Q V while the capacitor stores half Q V so exactly fifty percent is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of resistance value.

items.stem: Two fixed point charges, −5 nC on the left and +10 nC on the right, are 0.6 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.2 m from the −5 nC charge. Use the Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the resultant electric field at point P?
items.workedSolution: At P, both opposite-sign sources drive a positive test charge to the left. |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 1.12 × 10³ N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 562 N C⁻¹ (with r₂ = 0.4 m). Summing the two same-sense vectors gives E = 1.69 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (D).

markScheme.criterion: Adds same-direction inverse-square contributions to obtain 1.69 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (D).

items.stem: Fixed point charges +4 nC (left) and +10 nC (right) are separated by 0.7 m in free space. A probe charge of −2.4 nC is held at point P, 0.3 m from the +4 nC charge. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², with V = 0 at infinity. What is the electric potential at P due to the two fixed charges?
items.workedSolution: Electric potential at P depends only on the source charges: V = k(q₁/0.3 + q₂/0.4) = 120 V + (225 V) = 345 V (D).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = k(q₁/0.3 + q₂/0.4) = 345 V (D), independent of q_test.

items.stem: Two point charges, +12 nC on the left and −3 nC on the right, are fixed 0.3 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line to the right of both charges, 0.5 m from the +12 nC charge. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the resultant electric field at point P?
items.workedSolution: Exterior point P is r₁ = 0.5 m to the right of +12 nC and r₂ = 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.2 m to the right of −3 nC. Superposing E_x = kq₁/r₁² + kq₂/r₂² gives 243 N C⁻¹ to the left (D).

markScheme.criterion: Uses r₁ = 0.5 m and r₂ = 0.2 m to obtain 243 N C⁻¹ to the left (D).

items.stem: Two point charges, +1 nC on the left and +9 nC on the right, are fixed 0.8 m apart in a vacuum. Calculate the distance from the +1 nC charge to the point between them where the resultant electric field is zero.
items.workedSolution: Equating opposing field magnitudes gives q₁/x² = q₂/(0.8 − x)², so (0.8 − x)/x = √(9/1). Solving yields x = 0.8 × √1/(√1 + √9) = 0.200 m (A).

markScheme.criterion: Equates kq₁/x² = kq₂/(0.8 − x)² to obtain x = 0.200 m (A).

items.stem: Two point charges are fixed on the x-axis in a vacuum: +8 nC at x = 0 and +2 nC at x = 0.5 m. Point P lies on the axis at x = 0.2 m. A small test charge of −2 nC is placed at P without moving the fixed charges. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Calculate the resultant electric force on the −2 nC test charge.
items.workedSolution: At P (r₁ = 0.2 m, r₂ = 0.3 m), the resultant electric field is E = 1.60 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right. Multiplying by q_test = −2 nC gives F = q_test E = 3.20 × 10⁻⁶ N to the left (C).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates E = 1.60 × 10³ N C⁻¹ and F = qE = 3.20 × 10⁻⁶ N to the left (C).

items.stem: In a uniform electric field, three parallel equipotential surfaces are separated by 0.05 m. Their potentials from left to right are 360 V, 200 V, and 40 V. A particle of charge −1.25 × 10⁻⁸ C moves from the 360 V line to the 40 V line. Calculate the signed work done by the electric field on the charge.
items.workedSolution: Work done by the electric field is W_field = q(V_initial − V_final) = (−1.25 × 10⁻⁸ C)(360 − (40)) = −4.00 × 10⁻⁶ J (A).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates W_field = q(V_i − V_f) = −4.00 × 10⁻⁶ J (A).

items.stem: An alpha particle of charge +2e approaches a stationary uranium nucleus of charge +92e head-on. Their minimum centre-to-centre separation is 6 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and zero electric potential at infinity. What is the electric potential due to the uranium nucleus at distance r_min?
items.workedSolution: Radial potential of the +92e nucleus is V = kZe / r_min = (8.99 × 10⁹ × 92 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) / (6 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 2.21 × 10⁶ V (B).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = kZe / r_min = 2.21 × 10⁶ V (B).

items.stem: Two fixed point charges of +3 nC (left) and +27 nC (right) are separated by 0.9 m in free space. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², with zero potential at infinity. Calculate the electric potential at the point between the charges where the resultant electric field is zero.
items.workedSolution: Zero field occurs at x = 0.9 × √3/(√3 + √27) = 0.225 m from +3 nC (and 0.675 m from +27 nC). Scalar potentials add: V = k(q₁/x + q₂/(d − x)) = 479 V (C).

markScheme.criterion: Finds x = 0.225 m and sums positive scalar potentials to obtain 479 V (C).

items.stem: An oil droplet of mass $8.05 \times 10^{-15}\text{ kg}$ carrying a net charge of $9.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$ is held completely stationary between horizontal parallel plates. Taking $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$, what uniform electric field strength $E$ is required to balance the droplet?
items.workedSolution: Stationary balance gives $QE = mg \Rightarrow E = \frac{mg}{Q} = \frac{8.05 \times 10^{-15} \times 9.81}{9.60 \times 10^{-19}} = 8.22 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 8.22 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.

items.stem: An isolated metal sphere of radius 20.0 cm is charged to a potential of 45.0 kV ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F m}^{-1}$). Using $C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 R$ and $E = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$, calculate the electrostatic energy stored on the sphere in millijoules.

markScheme.criterion: Finds C = 22.2 pF and E = 22.5 mJ.

items.stem: Two point charges, +9Q on the left and +5Q on the right, are fixed a distance 3 x apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line between them, 2 x from the left charge. Using the Coulomb constant k, express the resultant electric field at P in terms of kQ/x².
items.workedSolution: At P, +9Q produces (9/2²) kQ/x² = 2.25 kQ/x² to the right, while +5Q at distance 1 x produces (5/1²) kQ/x² = 5.00 kQ/x² to the left. Net field = 2.75 kQ/x² to the left (C).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts (9/2²) and (5/1²) to obtain 2.75 kQ/x² to the left (C).

items.stem: Two point charges lie on the x-axis in a vacuum: q₁ = 2 × 10⁻⁹ C at x = 0 and an unknown charge q₂ at x = 1 m. The resultant electric field is zero at x = 0.2 m. Calculate the magnitude ratio |q₂ / q₁|.
items.workedSolution: At x₀ = 0.2 m, the distance from q₂ is d − x₀ = 0.8 m. Setting |q₁|/x₀² = |q₂|/(d − x₀)² gives |q₂/q₁| = (0.8/0.2)² = 16.0 (D).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ((d − x₀)/x₀)² = (0.8/0.2)² = 16.0 (D).

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates in a vacuum are 0.05 m apart, with a potential difference of 800 V between them. A deuteron (m = 3.34 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, q = +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) starts from rest and accelerates across the uniform electric field. Neglecting gravity, calculate the speed of the deuteron when it reaches the 0 V plate.
items.workedSolution: By conservation of energy, ½mv² = qV, so v = √(2qV / m) = √(2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 800 / 3.34 × 10⁻²⁷) = 2.77 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (B).

markScheme.criterion: Equates ½mv² = qV to obtain v = 2.77 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: Two point charges of −6 nC and −3 nC are fixed 0.6 m apart in a vacuum, with −6 nC on the left. Point P lies on the line between them, 0.2 m from the left charge. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Calculate the magnitude and direction of the resultant electric field at point P.
items.workedSolution: Between like-sign charges, the individual fields at P oppose each other: |E₁| = k|q₁|/(0.2)² = 1.35 × 10³ N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/(0.4)² = 169 N C⁻¹. Subtracting gives |E_net| = 1.18 × 10³ N C⁻¹ directed to the left (B).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts opposing inverse-square field contributions to obtain 1.18 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (B).

items.stem: Two fixed point charges lie on the x-axis: +2 nC at x = 0 and −8 nC at x = 0.5 m. Point P lies between them at x = 0.1 m, where the electric potential is zero. Take 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electric potential at infinity. Determine the resultant electric field at point P.
items.workedSolution: Even though V = kq₁/r₁ + kq₂/r₂ = 0 at P, the potential gradient dV/dx is non-zero because both opposite charges drive a positive test charge to the right: E = 1.80 × 10³ N C⁻¹ + 449 N C⁻¹ = 2.25 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (B).

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes E != 0 when V = 0 and adds the field contributions along the line to obtain 2.25 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (B).

items.stem: Two parallel metal plates are 0.045 m apart in a vacuum, with a potential difference of 360 V across them. A charged particle (q = +5 × 10⁻⁸ C, m = 2 × 10⁻⁶ kg) moves from the positive plate to the 0 V plate. Calculate the work done by the electric field on the particle as it moves from the 360 V plate to the 0 V plate.
items.workedSolution: Electrical work done across the full potential difference is W = qΔV = (5 × 10⁻⁸)(360) = 1.80 × 10⁻⁵ J (C).

items.stem: Three parallel vertical equipotential lines lie in a uniform electric field, spaced 0.05 m apart. From left to right, their potentials are 240 V, 140 V, and 40 V. A charged bead of mass 2 × 10⁻⁵ kg and charge +4 × 10⁻⁸ C starts from rest on the middle 140 V line. It moves horizontally without friction to the 40 V line. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the uniform electric field.
items.workedSolution: Electric field points toward decreasing potential (to the right) with magnitude E = |ΔV|/s = (140 − 40) / 0.05 = 2.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right (B).

markScheme.criterion: Uses E = −ΔV/Δx to obtain 2.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right (B).

items.stem: Electrons released from the cold cathode of a low-pressure gas-discharge tube accelerate across a potential difference of $4.50\text{ kV}$ toward the anode. Neglecting relativistic effects and gas collisions, calculate the maximum speed of the cathode-ray electrons.
items.workedSolution: From $\frac{1}{2}m_{\text{e}}v^2 = eV$, $v = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 4500}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}}} = 3.98 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 3.98 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Two point charges, −8 nC on the left and −5 nC on the right, are held 0.7 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies between them at a distance of 0.3 m from the left charge. Assume a vacuum with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero potential at infinity. What is the electric potential at point P?
items.workedSolution: Electric potential is a signed scalar: V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂) with r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.4 m. Thus V = −240 V + (−112 V) = −352 V (D).

markScheme.criterion: Sums signed scalar potentials kq₁/0.3 + kq₂/0.4 = −352 V (D).

items.stem: An uncharged capacitor is connected through a series resistor R to an ideal constant-emf battery of voltage V until fully charged to charge Q. What happens to the energy transferred by the battery?
items.workedSolution: The battery supplies energy Q V while the capacitor stores half Q V so exactly fifty percent is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of resistance value. Therefore the correct statement is: The battery supplies energy Q V while the capacitor stores half Q V so exactly fifty percent is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of resistance value

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: battery supplies energy Q V while the capacitor stores half Q V so exactly fifty percent is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of resistance value.

options.text: The battery supplies energy half Q V which is stored with one hundred percent efficiency when resistance is small.
options.distractorRationale: Battery work is W = QV, not ½QV, and 50% is always dissipated regardless of R.

options.label: B
options.text: The fraction dissipated as thermal energy rises toward one hundred percent as the series resistor R is made larger.
options.distractorRationale: Larger R slows charging (longer τ = RC) but total energy lost ∫I²R dt remains ½QV.

options.label: C
options.text: The battery supplies energy Q V while the capacitor stores half Q V so exactly fifty percent is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of resistance value

options.label: D
options.text: The capacitor stores the full Q V supplied by the battery while circuit resistance stores zero energy.
options.distractorRationale: Area under the linear Q–V graph is only half the rectangle QV.

items.stem: Two point charges of −9 nC and +4 nC are fixed 0.5 m apart on a horizontal line, with −9 nC on the left. Point P lies between them, 0.3 m from the left charge. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the resultant electric field at point P?
items.workedSolution: At P, both opposite-sign sources drive a positive test charge to the left. |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 899 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 899 N C⁻¹ (with r₂ = 0.2 m). Summing the two same-sense vectors gives E = 1.80 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (B).

markScheme.criterion: Adds same-direction inverse-square contributions to obtain 1.80 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (B).

items.stem: Point charges +4 nC and +6 nC are fixed 0.5 m apart on a horizontal line, with +4 nC on the left. Point P lies on the same line, 0.8 m to the right of +4 nC. Use the Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Determine the resultant electric field at point P.
items.workedSolution: Exterior point P is r₁ = 0.8 m to the right of +4 nC and r₂ = 0.8 − 0.5 = 0.3 m to the right of +6 nC. Superposing E_x = kq₁/r₁² + kq₂/r₂² gives 656 N C⁻¹ to the right (A).

markScheme.criterion: Uses r₁ = 0.8 m and r₂ = 0.3 m to obtain 656 N C⁻¹ to the right (A).

items.stem: Two point charges are fixed on the x-axis in a vacuum: +3 nC at x = 0 and +12 nC at x = 0.6 m. Calculate the distance x from the +3 nC charge to the point between them where the electric field is zero.
items.workedSolution: Equating opposing field magnitudes gives q₁/x² = q₂/(0.6 − x)², so (0.6 − x)/x = √(12/3). Solving yields x = 0.6 × √3/(√3 + √12) = 0.200 m (D).

markScheme.criterion: Equates kq₁/x² = kq₂/(0.6 − x)² to obtain x = 0.200 m (D).

items.stem: Two fixed point charges of +4 nC (left) and −6 nC (right) are 0.4 m apart in a vacuum. Point P lies on the line joining them, 0.15 m from the left charge. A small test charge of −3.2 nC is placed at P without moving the fixed charges. Use the Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Calculate the resultant electric force on the −3.2 nC test charge.
items.workedSolution: At P (r₁ = 0.15 m, r₂ = 0.25 m), the resultant electric field is E = 2.46 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right. Multiplying by q_test = −3.2 nC gives F = q_test E = 7.88 × 10⁻⁶ N to the left (D).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates E = 2.46 × 10³ N C⁻¹ and F = qE = 7.88 × 10⁻⁶ N to the left (D).

items.stem: The right-hand graph shows electric potential V against radial distance r outside a positively charged conducting sphere. How is the electric field strength E determined from this curve?
items.workedSolution: Because E = −ΔV/Δr (magnitude ΔV/Δr on the AQA Data Sheet), the steepness of the V–r curve gives field strength directly. Therefore the correct statement is: Relating the two graphs, field strength equals the negative gradient of the potential versus distance graph, so the steepest potential gradient occurs closest to the surface.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: field strength equals the negative gradient of the potential versus distance graph, so the steepest potential gradient occurs closest to the surface.

options.label: A
options.text: Relating the two graphs, field strength equals the negative gradient of the potential versus distance graph, so the steepest potential gradient occurs closest to the surface.

options.label: B
options.text: Electric field strength equals the area enclosed beneath the potential versus distance curve from the sphere surface to r.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses differentiation and integration: area under E–r gives ΔV, whereas gradient of V–r gives E.

options.label: C
options.text: Electric field strength equals the ratio V/r at every point along a radial field curve.
options.distractorRationale: Although V/r happens to match kQ/r² for a single isolated point charge, the general physical relation from any V–r graph is the tangent gradient −ΔV/Δr.

options.label: D
options.text: Electric field strength equals the reciprocal of the tangent gradient, −Δr/ΔV.
options.distractorRationale: Units of Δr/ΔV are m V⁻¹, the inverse of field strength V m⁻¹.

items.stem: Three parallel equipotential lines lie in a uniform electric field, spaced 0.025 m apart. From left to right, their potentials are 250 V, 150 V, and 50 V. A test charge of +6 × 10⁻⁹ C moves from the leftmost surface (250 V) to the rightmost surface (50 V). Calculate the signed change in electric potential energy ΔE_p of the charge.
items.workedSolution: Change in electric potential energy is ΔE_p = q(V_final − V_initial) = (+6 × 10⁻⁹ C)(50 − (250)) = −1.20 × 10⁻⁶ J (B).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p = q(V_f − V_i) = −1.20 × 10⁻⁶ J (B).

items.stem: A stationary nickel nucleus of charge +28e repels a triply charged lithium nucleus of charge +3e approaching head-on. The incoming particle comes to rest at a separation of 3.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and zero electric potential at infinity. Calculate the electrostatic potential energy of the system at closest approach, in electronvolts (eV).
items.workedSolution: At r_min, V = kZe / r_min = 1.15 × 10⁶ V. For a +3e projectile, E_p = 3eV = 3.45 × 10⁶ eV (D).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = 1.15 × 10⁶ V and E_p = 3V (in eV) = 3.45 × 10⁶ eV (D).

items.stem: Two fixed point charges of +9 nC (left) and +1 nC (right) are separated by 0.5 m in free space. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electric potential at infinity. Calculate the electric potential at the point between the charges where the resultant electric field is zero.
items.workedSolution: Zero field occurs at x = 0.5 × √9/(√9 + √1) = 0.375 m from +9 nC (and 0.125 m from +1 nC). Scalar potentials add: V = k(q₁/x + q₂/(d − x)) = 288 V (D).

markScheme.criterion: Finds x = 0.375 m and sums positive scalar potentials to obtain 288 V (D).

items.stem: In a Millikan oil-drop experiment with the electric field switched off, an oil droplet of density 880 kg m⁻³ falls at a terminal speed of 1.10 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹. The viscosity of air is 1.81 × 10⁻⁵ Pa s. Neglecting air upthrust and taking $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$, calculate the radius of the droplet.
items.workedSolution: Equating Stokes drag and weight: $6\pi\eta r v = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho g \Rightarrow r = \sqrt{\frac{9\eta v}{2\rho g}} = \sqrt{\frac{9 \times 1.81 \times 10^{-5} \times 1.10 \times 10^{-4}}{2 \times 880 \times 9.81}} = 1.02 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m} = 1.02 μm$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 1.02 μm.

items.stem: An isolated conducting dome of a Van de Graaff generator has radius 15.0 cm. Taking $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F m}^{-1}$ and using $C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 R$, calculate its capacitance in picofarads.

markScheme.criterion: Applies C = 4πε₀R to obtain 16.7 pF.

items.stem: Two positive point charges, +5Q and +4Q, are fixed a distance 3 x apart in a vacuum, with +5Q on the left. Point P lies between them at a distance 2 x from +5Q. Using the Coulomb constant k, express the resultant electric field at P in terms of kQ/x².
items.workedSolution: At P, +5Q produces (5/2²) kQ/x² = 1.25 kQ/x² to the right, while +4Q at distance 1 x produces (4/1²) kQ/x² = 4.00 kQ/x² to the left. Net field = 2.75 kQ/x² to the left (A).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts (5/2²) and (4/1²) to obtain 2.75 kQ/x² to the left (A).

items.stem: Point charges q₁ = 4 × 10⁻⁹ C (left) and q₂ (right) are fixed 0.6 m apart in a vacuum. The resultant electric field is zero at a point between them, 0.2 m to the right of q₁. Calculate the signed value of charge q₂.
items.workedSolution: An interior null point requires q₁ and q₂ to have the same sign (+). Equating kq₁/x₀² = kq₂/(d − x₀)² with d − x₀ = 0.4 m gives q₂ = q₁((0.4)/(0.2))² = 4.00 × 4 × 10⁻⁹ C = +1.60 × 10⁻⁸ C (A).

markScheme.criterion: Uses q₂ = q₁((d − x₀)/x₀)² with positive sign to obtain +1.60 × 10⁻⁸ C (A).
